column1: Mimicking

Can you describe the smelliest person you have met? I've met many people, so it's a difficult question. Nevertheless, one person sticks vividly in my mind. I was a college student at the time waiting for a connecting bus from the University of the West Indies to go to the city. The transport hub was overcrowded and I had my nose buried in a dog-eared copy of *The Metamorphosis*. A man, middle-aged, dressed in what I would assume were once clean clothes but had clearly not been washed in weeks, maybe months, squeezed onto the bench beside me. The first impression was always visual, his clothes appeared, to my inexperienced eyes, to be a mixture of faded colours and indeterminate stains. This initial impression was soon overwhelmed by the olfactory assault that followed. The odour was complex, a symphony of neglect and desperation. It consisted of a base note of unwashed body odour. This was then overlaid with the acrid smell of stale sweat, a harsh reminder of physical exertion and inadequate hygiene. This noxious combination was then further complicated by the inclusion of what I would call 'environmental' smells: the pervasive aroma of the streets, mixed with the faint, cloying stench of what might have been rotting food or refuse. One of my most vivid memories of this encounter was the way the smell seemed to cling. It didn't just hang in the air, it permeated the very fabric of the bus stop, a lasting testament to a harsh existence that clearly didn't value the basics of cleanliness. I kept my book pressed close to my face, hoping, in vain, that it would serve as some kind of olfactory filter. I couldn't wait to get to the city to escape that lingering malodorous encounter.

What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? I have been fortunate enough to have the opportunity to hear some choice comments from medical professionals over the years. One stands out. I had recently moved to a new city and was in search of a general practitioner. This was before I was an adult and I wasn't too careful in choosing one. On the recommendation of a friend I went to a doctor who was renowned for his high-powered efficiency. The waiting room had the most imposing sense of order I had ever seen in a doctor's office. Every chair was perfectly positioned, every magazine was neatly stacked and the staff behind the desk all appeared to be graduates of the same modeling school. It felt like I was in a military installation. I went in, got the routine checks and was about to leave. The doctor stopped me and asked me for a small favor. He wanted to see what my natural gait was like and asked me to walk in a circle in his office. I did so, somewhat puzzled. He then told me to sit down. 'You have a problem with one of your feet,' he said. 'I can see it in your walk. You need to get that taken care of.' I explained to him that I was feeling fine and had no issues. He gave a dismissive hand gesture, 'Whether you feel something or not doesn't matter. It's there. You need to go see a podiatrist.' I thanked him and left the clinic. I never went back. I was young and foolish. I should have asked for his credentials. I should have put his practice to the test and made him explain, in detail, what physical abnormality he observed. I should have asked him to compare my gait with that of a hundred other patients and how it stood up to clinical testing. He caught me at a bad time. I was distracted and preoccupied with other pressing concerns. I lacked the confidence and composure to properly test him. I ended up doing nothing about it. It wasn't the only time I was given a medical misdiagnosis. I just have to laugh at it all now.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? I am a nerdy man. My high school classmates would have readily described me as such. I am a big proponent of the merits of the nerdy lifestyle. However, in keeping with the question. I believe the nerdy lifestyle would attract as many detractors as it attracted supporters. Firstly most ‘nerdy’ men don’t really fit any aesthetic description of a “man”. Many people, men and women alike, are attracted to the aesthetics of the body i.e. height, facial, broad shoulders, narrow waist, athleticism, fashion, and grooming. If those things are not prioritized then you will have a hard time attracting the fairer sex or even many of your own sex. In relation to fashion and grooming many nerdy men I have met are not just fashion-inept; they are outright antagonistic to any form of personal grooming and appearance. I remember once when I was much younger, there was an intense heatwave throughout Trinidad and Tobago. There were lots of power outages, and I was at my friend’s house along with a bunch of others. Our AC was off, beads of sweat rolling down our shirts, and we still had to stay in the house. The power was switched on, and I went to turn on his mother's very expensive AC unit. A friend said: "You can't turn on this AC. You have to get out of the house like, NOW!" I was taken aback: "Why?" And, he answered me: "Have you seen the way you look? Your hair sticking up, unwashed face, smelling all... just... just get out of here and go shower." And then it dawned on me that I had spent the entire day immersed in a PC game and had forgotten to bathe or groom or care about anything whatsoever. Many people, women, and men, care about these factors. Then there is the lack of basic social skills. Nerdy people are often introverted and that’s not a problem. Some of the most successful people I know in terms of wealth and happiness are highly introverted and shy. However, when the introversion is mixed with a lack of basic social skills, this can create a very off-putting personality. For example, the ‘mansplaining’ trait. The tendency to explain things in a condescending and overly detailed and sometimes incorrect way can alienate people very quickly. This can happen with women as well as men. Lack of understanding of basic social cues such as body language, tone of voice, the ability to read a room can make the conversation and company unpleasant. Furthermore, I note that the ‘nerd/geek’ persona is usually associated with a certain obsession that can sometimes be off-putting. The propensity of many nerdy men to talk non-stop about their singular specific interests without any form of self-awareness is a factor. I have talked to many of my female friends about the traits and behaviors of men that they find unappealing. They have often mentioned (without prompting) that even when they try to engage in a conversation about these obsessions with the man, the man acts with complete obliviousness and seems simply content to talk about his singular obsession with no regard for the woman’s reaction or interest. It would make the woman feel insignificant and ‘unheard’. In conclusion, many women (and men) may “hate” nerdy men simply based on poor personal presentation, deficient social skills and a propensity for obsessiveness.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? I've always been a bit of a snob when it comes to judging a movie by its poster. It's a terrible habit, I know, but I can't help it. The marketing department has a huge role to play in my decision of whether or not to spend money and time on a film. A bad poster can signal a bad movie, even if the film turns out to be a hidden gem. A great poster, or a movie poster that speaks to me, can sway me. It's like forming a first impression.  Here are a few examples:  *   **Anything with a floating head.** I've gotten a lot better when it comes to avoiding these. It screams lazy, generic, and uninspired. These tend to be big-budget action films, romantic comedies, or horror flicks with a predictable plot. Think of the poster for *The Call* (2020). It was probably a decent Korean thriller, but the poster - Halle Berry’s detached head against a generic backdrop, with one or two other actors, their faces floating to the sides as if in outer space - made it instantly forgettable. The same can be said of 90% of Liam Neeson action movies. There is no reason to go out of your way to see it. *   **Movies with a too-busy poster.** These are the ones where they cram every single character and explosion onto the poster to trick you into thinking the movie has breadth and depth when in reality it’s just another unoriginal blockbuster. In order to save money graphic designers will usually opt for using the most generic of fonts. Another great example of this phenomenon is the *Transformers* franchise. I find those posters to be a cacophony of noise with little artistic merit. They'll overload your senses, making you think you're about to experience an epic, but it's usually just an assault on the eyes that sets the tone for what's to come. *   **Movies with a poster featuring a celebrity face that's nothing like the character.** This happens more often than you’d think. Sometimes the studio will choose a celebrity who has no resemblance to the character described in the source material. The poster then becomes a blatant attempt to cash in on the celebrity's popularity, rather than to accurately represent the film. Case in point, *Death on the Nile* (2022). Gal Gadot's presence on that poster made absolutely no sense to me especially given the fact that the movie and her performance was lacklustre.  All in all, a good movie poster should be a work of art that captures the essence of the film without giving away too much of the plot. It should be intriguing, visually appealing, and make you want to see the movie. I still fall for bad movie posters from time to time. It happens to the best of us. However, I've wised up over the years. Nowadays I tend to judge a movie by its trailer, reviews and recommendations. Nevertheless it still is a bad habit.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? The lowest probability event I have ever personally witnessed? Probably the time I was in the audience of a live televised awards show. No, I was not a celebrity, a nominee or even a plus-one. I was just a regular guy who had somehow finagled his way inside. It was a major awards show, the kind with all the glitz, glamour, and celebrities in designer outfits smiling for photographers. I was merely in the audience, a nobody amidst the 'somebodies.' I was there through a confluence of unlikely circumstances and a series of fortunate coincidences, each with a probability so slim that I still struggle to believe it happened. It involved an old university friend who worked as a stagehand, a misplaced guest pass, and a serious disregard for security protocols. The whole affair felt like a fever dream. It was a masterclass in how to exploit loopholes in a system. I was, in any case, seated among the hoi polloi, the paying public, and the significant others of the production crew, but I was *in*.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? This is a contentious issue, and my take is necessarily nuanced. On one hand, I firmly believe in the spirit of inclusivity and the right to compete. Transgender athletes, like any other group, should be afforded the opportunity to pursue their athletic dreams. However, the biological realities of gender, particularly in the context of a sport like boxing, cannot be ignored. The fundamental differences in bone density, muscle mass, and hormonal profiles between men and women, established over millennia of evolution, are significant. To deny this would be intellectually dishonest. To allow a male, even one who has undergone some form of transition, to compete against biological women, jeopardizes the fairness of the competition and, frankly, puts female athletes at a physical disadvantage, and potentially, at risk. It's a delicate balancing act, this intersection of fairness, inclusion, and safety. Regulations must prioritize the safety and well-being of all competitors. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) needs to continually review and update its guidelines, ensuring that they are based on the best scientific evidence. And what about the athletes themselves? Are they consulted or are they simply subjects in a debate of ideology? A great deal more needs to be done than the current lip service about ‘inclusion’ before this is truly fair. The current criteria appear to be more performative than effective. Someone is going to get hurt and when that happens, and it will eventually, who takes responsibility?

Has your friend ever saved your life? I wouldn't exactly say “saved my life”, but I do have a friend whose actions played a critical role in preventing a disastrous situation. We were in our early twenties, embarking on that rite of passage known as the ‘grand backpacking adventure through Europe’. We were in Italy. Rome, to be exact, smack dab in the middle of the Eternal City's most raucous district. Upon the insistence of my friend (let’s call him Dave), we decided to patronize a bar some kilometres away from our dingy, cheap, and rather undesirable hostel. Dave had an unerring knack for finding ‘off the beaten path’ establishments that were, shall we say, more attuned to the tastes of the locals than the typical tourist-frequented dives. This particular bar, a dimly lit cellar-like establishment, was packed with boisterous locals, all engaged in raucous conversations, gesturing wildly and drinking with conspicuous enthusiasm at the bar. This was Italy, after all, the land of wine, song, and passionate people. We had each had a couple of drinks and were having a whale of a time, laughing and gesticulating along with the locals, although we barely understood a word of what was being said. After a while, Dave excused himself to go to the bathroom. He was gone for quite some time, so I decided to go look for him. I found him outside, in a dark alleyway, and, from what I could gather from the shouts and angry gestures of the locals, he had just had a heated argument with a few of them. I asked him what was going on. He confessed that he had accidentally bumped into someone, spilling his drink in the process. I knew Dave. He was a bit of a klutz and also a bit of a smart aleck. Neither the clumsy nature nor the sass helped in this instance. The locals’ tone and movements suggested that this was not just a simple matter of spilled drinks. I managed to communicate, through wildly animated gestures and a few of the Italian words I had picked up, that we were sorry and that it was merely an accident. I then offered to pay for their drinks. This just seemed to make things worse. They were adamant, and even more irate, that this wasn't a situation that could be casually resolved with a few euros. I could sense that they were about to do something that neither Dave nor I would have enjoyed. I was about to panic when Dave piped up in fluent Italian (I never knew he could speak the language). He did some fast talking and the situation diffused… somewhat. We were chased, but we escaped.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? When I was a teenager, in my small Caribbean island nation, I worked at a KFC. The experience wasn’t quite life-altering in the classical sense, no epiphany that caused an immediate change in lifestyle, but the memories are still very vivid, as if it happened just yesterday. The pay was dreadful, the hours long, the customers often rude, and the management generally clueless, but it was a crucible of sorts, a pressure cooker where you learned about human nature, the value of a hard earned dollar, and the importance of teamwork.  Working the front counter, there was the incessant hum of the fryers, the constant chatter, the smell of fried chicken (which, after a time, you learn to despise), and the stream of customers, each with their own story, their own needs, their own moods. There were the regulars, the ones you'd come to know by name and order; the families out for a treat; the tourists, wide-eyed and bewildered by our local lingo; the late-night crowd, fueled by alcohol and questionable intentions. They all came to us. You'd see the same faces every day. I vividly remember being a part of those interactions and how they shaped my perspective on life.  It wasn’t glamorous. But it was real. It was a masterclass in patience, in problem-solving, in the art of customer service, and in the sheer absurdity of the human condition. I wouldn’t trade those early fast-food years for anything, and often find myself wistfully musing on the lessons I learned while flipping burgers and serving up chicken.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? One of the most common mistakes in filmmaking is a promising premise botched by a terrible script. Often a movie has everything going for it: a stellar cast, a visionary director, a huge budget, and great special effects. But, when all the pieces fail to cohere due to a weak narrative, the whole enterprise collapses. This happened with the 1998 film *Sphere*. The movie had Dustin Hoffman, Samuel L. Jackson, Sharon Stone, and a screenplay adapted from a Michael Crichton novel. The book was a bestseller, and the cast were all acclaimed actors. But the writing… oh, the writing. Another example of a terrible script ruining a potentially great movie is *Cats* (2019). The musical has a devoted following and the theatrical production is still running in many countries. However, the film adaptation was an unmitigated disaster. The CGI was off-putting, the songs were poorly arranged, and the plot made no sense. This movie could have worked with even a halfway decent script. Bad scripts seem to plague superhero films and have sadly afflicted some of the greatest directors of all time. For instance, *Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice* (2016) had an all-star cast, including Ben Affleck as Batman, and was directed by Zack Snyder. But the screenplay was convoluted and nonsensical. Audiences and critics alike lambasted it, and deservedly so. The movie had so much potential, featuring two of the most iconic superheroes facing off against each other. *Terminator: Dark Fate* (2019) had a similar problem. The movie had Linda Hamilton, Arnold Schwarzenegger, and James Cameron producing. Yet, the script was just… bad. The plot was uninspired and the writing weak. The movie failed at the box office, despite the high expectations of fans of the franchise. Screenwriting is the foundation on which all other elements of a movie rest. It's the most important part of moviemaking and a bad script can kill a film.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? The biggest anticlimax in movie history? For me, it's the ending of *War of the Worlds* (2005). I understand that the novel, upon which the movie is based, also had the same anticlimactic ending, but I still can't get over it, especially given the sheer amount of spectacle and hype the movie built up to. The Martians, who had proven themselves capable of destroying entire cities with their advanced technology, are defeated by…a common cold. Honestly, it felt like a massive letdown after all the build-up. It's like watching a heavyweight boxing match, with both opponents beating the hell out of each other for 11 rounds and then, in the 12th round a judge steps in and announces that one of the fighters wins the fight because the other has a rash.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? I have a soft spot for *Catch Me If You Can* (2002). It’s one of those films that just grabs you from the opening scene and doesn’t let go. The story is compelling, based on the real-life exploits of Frank Abagnale Jr., a con artist who impersonated a pilot, a doctor, and a lawyer, all before he was of legal drinking age. What makes it such a captivating watch isn’t just the audacious nature of Abagnale's crimes but also the sheer artistry of the deception. The way he fabricated his personas, his mastery of forgery, and even his charisma – it's all depicted with such panache and style that you almost find yourself rooting for the guy, despite the illegality of his actions. Leonardo DiCaprio's portrayal of Abagnale is masterful; he perfectly embodies the character's youthful exuberance, resourcefulness, and underlying vulnerability. He’s incredibly convincing, especially given the rapid-fire changes in his character's identity. Tom Hanks as Carl Hanratty, the FBI agent pursuing him, is a superb foil. Their cat-and-mouse game is a central part of the movie's appeal, and the dialogue between the two is sharp, witty, and often surprisingly poignant. Director Steven Spielberg masterfully captures the era - the 1960s - with its stylish aesthetic, vibrant colors, and a jazzy, often upbeat soundtrack, further enhancing the viewing experience. It’s a film that manages to be both lighthearted and suspenseful, a rare combination that makes it a consistently enjoyable watch. Even though you know it's based on a true story, the sheer absurdity of it all is still hard to believe, which makes it even more fascinating. But beyond the charm and the cleverness, *Catch Me If You Can* offers a subtle commentary on the American dream, on ambition, and perhaps, on the blurred lines between fantasy and reality that seem to characterise this man's life and the essence of the ‘American dream' itself.

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? Yes, several times, and the accusations were as varied as the personalities of the accusers themselves. Once, a parent accused me of "favoritism" because I gave her child the only "B" in an otherwise stellar report card. Her argument was that her little darling was "gifted" and deserved special consideration. I tried to explain the rubric, the grading system, the hours I'd spent assessing his work fairly, but she was unconvinced, convinced instead that I was deliberately holding her son back, stunting his potential because... I don't know, maybe I envied his superior intellect? Another time, a student accused me of being too strict, of unjustly punishing him for "minor infractions" like talking during lessons or failing to hand in homework. He saw me as the enemy, a bureaucratic cog in the machine, seemingly hellbent on making his life miserable. He probably saw me as a joyless warden. Of course, I've also been accused, on occasion, of the opposite: of being "too lenient." This typically happened with students who felt they needed more discipline, more structure, more clear boundaries. These students craved the assurance that came with rules, with consequences, and when I strayed from the rigid path, they felt adrift. The truth is you’re always in a no-win situation. You’re damned if you do, damned if you don’t.

Why do some people not like Coldplay? Coldplay. Ah, Coldplay. The quintessential Marmite band. You either love them, or you find them to be the epitome of bland, anodyne, stadium-filling pop-rock. There is no middle ground. Personally, I’ve always found myself rather indifferent to their music. It's not that I actively dislike them, it's just… there. Existing, a sonic wallpaper, frequently encountered but rarely engaged with. They are, to me, perfectly pleasant. I've never felt the need to actively seek out a Coldplay song after their initial run of hits. Of course, there are many reasons why some find them unpalatable. For some it is the voice of Chris Martin himself; the gentle, almost ethereal tenor can grate on the ears. It’s a voice that perfectly suits the band's overall sound, but its lack of grit or edge can be a stumbling block for listeners seeking a dose of raw emotion. Then there is the question of lyrical depth, or lack thereof. Their songs are often criticised for being overly simplistic and generic, dealing in grand, sweeping statements of love, loss, and the pursuit of happiness – emotions that, delivered so straightforwardly can feel trite and contrived. They can also be accused of a certain musical predictability. Coldplay’s sound, though polished and radio-friendly, can lack the experimental flourishes that make other bands exciting. After a while, their song structure can feel formulaic. The slow build, the soaring chorus, the quiet bridge, the eventual crescendo – the overall package can become repetitive and ultimately, boring. And, let's not forget, their perceived pretentiousness. Coldplay are, undeniably, a hugely successful and critically acclaimed band. They are not afraid to make grandiose statements about the world, seemingly always striving for a higher purpose. This can be off-putting for their detractors. Some may view this as genuine artistic expression others as an exercise in self-importance.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? I'd have to say *The Terminal* (2004). I was expecting the usual saccharine, predictable fare from Spielberg, a director whose work, I've always contended, can waver from the sublime to the excruciating. While I appreciate his technical prowess—the man knows how to wield a camera and elicit strong performances from his actors—I tend to find his storytelling a bit on the nose, too heavy on the schmaltz. However, *The Terminal* completely defied my expectations. It's a film that should have failed spectacularly, given its seemingly flimsy premise: Viktor Navorski (Tom Hanks, in a role that feels tailor-made for him), a man from a fictional Eastern European country, gets stranded in JFK Airport’s international transit lounge due to a coup back in his homeland. The film's potential for a descent into mawkish sentimentality was immense. Yet, Spielberg masterfully navigates this treacherous terrain. The sheer ingenuity with which he crafts this world, transforming the airport into a microcosm of life itself, is remarkable. It's a testament to his skill as a filmmaker, his ability to find the extraordinary within the ordinary. The supporting cast, from the eternally underrated Stanley Tucci as the exasperated customs director to Catherine Zeta-Jones as the flight attendant with the unyielding stare, all deliver their roles with aplomb. The pacing is excellent; each scene is a carefully constructed brick that lays the foundation for the next, and the next until the final, satisfying conclusion. The film's exploration of themes – immigration, bureaucracy, longing for a connection, the absurdity of modern life and global politics—is handled elegantly. It is not an overt moralistic sermon but rather a gentle exploration of the human condition, laced with warmth and humour. It’s a film that resonates with you long after the credits roll, a reminder that even in the most sterile and impersonal of places, such as a bustling airport, the human spirit can find a way to flourish. *The Terminal* is precisely the kind of film Spielberg rarely makes, a film that, against all odds, manages to surprise and delight. It's a shining example of how simple stories, when told with skill and genuine heart, can resonate with profound depth.

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? There are a plethora of actors who have embraced the villainous mantle to chilling effect, but for me, the award, the *pièce de résistance*, if you will, goes to Alan Rickman. His portrayal of Hans Gruber in *Die Hard* is a masterclass in understated menace. He didn't need to sneer or rant; his power lay in his calm, collected demeanor. He offered a cold, calculating intelligence that outshone even the film's protagonist, John McClane. Rickman’s execution was flawless, he could deliver chilling, yet eloquent declarations while dressed in a tailor made suit. It's a testament to his skill that he often overshadowed Bruce Willis, a feat few actors can boast. Even more impressive? He managed something that few villains, especially action movie villains, can: garner the audience's respect. One can genuinely admire his composure and strategic acumen. Gruber was not a brute, but a sophisticated criminal for whom violence was a means to an end. You knew he could go from the witty repartee with McClane to cold, calculated murder in the blink of an eye, making him that much more terrifying. He was the epitome of the charming sociopath, the kind of villain you might actually want to grab a drink with, right before he stabs you in the back. Or, in Gruber's case, pushes you off a building. Truly, a magnificent performance that has set a gold standard for movie antagonists.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? When people start talking about how everything was "better" in their day. Look, I get it. Nostalgia is a powerful drug, and the sepia-toned haze of rose-tinted memories can be intoxicating. Maybe the music was "better" (debatable), the cars looked cooler (again, subjective), and the haircuts were... well, let's just say they were something. But to act as if the past was some utopian paradise, devoid of any of the problems that plague us today? Give me a break. It’s the same old song and dance, this selective amnesia, where every rose is without thorns. It's the equivalent of a seasoned lottery player telling you he can see into the future. It’s a sentiment that comes with a healthy dose of eye-rolling. And the worst part? It usually stems from a place of ignorance, a lack of critical reflection and an unwillingness to see the world as it truly is: complex, nuanced, and always, always changing. Whether it is the "good old days" when racism was blatant and accepted, or the bygone era when medical science was rudimentary, or the age when the internet did not exist (imagine that), these rose tinted glasses are often more blinding than enlightening. People who harp on about the "good old days" often do so because they are trying to avoid the present. They are desperate to escape the reality of their current situation, and so they retreat into the comforting fantasy of a time that never really was.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? During my time working as an usher, I was once reprimanded for not catching a couple of teenagers trying to sneak into another movie after theirs had finished. Now, bear in mind, this was in the late 90s, before the widespread adoption of smartphones. I'm talking about a time when the only way to know what movie was playing was to be present in the foyer, reading the posters. Anyway, these two kids, probably around 14 or 15, had exited their film and saw a crowd starting to form outside another cinema. The movie was just starting, they saw their opportunity and tried to blend in with the crowd. I immediately spotted them, not because they looked suspicious, but because I was paying particular attention. I knew those two faces. I’d taken their original tickets. This could mean money deducted from my measly pay! I stopped them at the door and asked to see their tickets. They sheepishly admitted they didn't have any, and I promptly escorted them out. Seemed simple enough. The next day my supervisor called me into his office. Apparently one of the teenagers had told his parents that I was refusing him and his friend entry to a film. Then they called the cinema, and the parent reported me to my supervisor. I didn’t deny the account to my boss; I gave him a full and frank account of the situation, and he took my side. I was lucky. The parent had clearly lied. However, the absurdity of the situation struck me: a teenager trying to watch a movie for free, and the parents backing them up. And it was the teenager, the perpetrator of the infraction, who had complained to the authorities, the cinema management.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? I've had a couple of these over the years. The first was a sales and marketing position at a small company in the manufacturing sector. The interview process itself was a circus. There were three rounds of interviews, each with a different person, and I was told that I would be working directly with a third. That felt off but the job seemed perfect at the time. It promised a base salary that beat my expectations, plus commission, car allowance, and a host of other incentives. The role was going to be a senior sales manager, something I'd been working toward for years. All told, the job would've been a game-changer compared to my then-current situation. However, during the final interview, I got the distinct impression that there was a tremendous amount of internal conflict and discord. The person I was interviewing with spent a good hour badmouthing all her colleagues and making complaints about the direction of the company. Looking back, I should've immediately realized that the company's problems were deeply rooted and that the role would have been nothing but stress from the get go. I ignored that warning sign. Then, there was the second time. It wasn’t exactly a red flag but rather a yellow caution. The recruiter was too eager to throw praise at me. I was being told that I was perfect, the best candidate they had seen, and they were going to go to bat for me. It felt all a little bit too convenient, too smooth. Now, I've learned that when it smells good like a perfume advertisement, chances are it will smell bad in reality. Sure enough, I accepted the offer. The organization as a whole was a basket case. I probably would've been better off if I'd trusted my intuition and walked away, but I stuck around for far longer than I should’ve. The entire experience left a bad taste in my mouth and provided me with a valuable and painful lesson about how to spot and avoid future career pitfalls.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? I believe the "golden age" of cinema is a meaningless concept. Most people seem to arbitrarily place it somewhere between the mid-1960s and early 1980s. For all its supposed merits and artistic integrity, it's still primarily nostalgia talking. Cinema, as a form of art, reflects the era in which it's made. The technology, moral sensibilities, and the very anxieties of a period are all embedded within it. Therefore, a film from 1975, say, is inherently a film of 1975. The "golden age" is simply a convenient label attached to a period of filmmaking that now feels more relatable to those generations who grew up with it. It's the same as any other artistic medium. You go into a museum, and you'll find Renaissance paintings; the 18th-century French Salon period; the Cubist or Dada movements; or the more contemporary movements. Each period has its own aesthetic, and the films of Hollywood or Europe during the so-called "golden age" are just another chapter in this continuing artistic progression. They are no more inherently superior than the films being made today. A better film is a better film, regardless of when it was made. Often, there are significant technological limitations that restrict the stories that can be told and the ways in which they can be told. Black and white, for example, is beautiful, but it's a limitation for filmmakers in a way that colour is not. Special effects were also laughably bad compared to what's achievable today. And whilst there's always been bad movies, the sheer volume of content being produced today means there is simply more good stuff to discover. Some of the greatest performances, stories, and visuals are being created right now. We will look back on this time with the same selective nostalgia as many do of the so-called "golden age". Of course, I also hold the unpopular opinion that every James Cameron film is pure, unadulterated gold, but that's a story for another time.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? My life, like most, has had its fair share of valleys. Not as dramatic as a sudden, precipitous collapse, more of a slow, insidious descent into a fog of disillusionment. There’s no singular picture that perfectly encapsulates that; no defining photograph captures the nuances of a gradual erosion of hope. It’s rarely a dramatic event but an accumulation of minor setbacks. A series of small disappointments. It's less a snapshot and more of a collage. If I absolutely had to choose, it's a series of blurred images. Pictures that I would have to piece together from my memories. One would be me, staring blankly at a computer screen, the glow reflecting in my vacant eyes, the ambient temperature seems to be the only warmth I can feel, the deadlines looming like vultures, my dreams of a fulfilling career reduced to a mere echo. The second would be the cramped, windowless apartment, the stale air thick with the scent of cheap instant noodles and unfulfilled potential; one that I felt as if I was unable to escape from. Sunlight had become a distant memory. The third would be my reflection in the mirror, a stranger with tired eyes betraying a despair I tried, and usually failed, to mask. That face was haunted, not by a single ghost, but a legion. Yet even those fragmented images don't fully capture the essence of that low point. It’s not about the physical surroundings, or the outward appearances. It's about the internal desolation, the quiet desperation, and the gradual numbing of the soul. Perhaps that photo doesn't exist. Perhaps the only true image is the understanding that while it’s difficult to imagine, the only way to go is up.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? I felt bad for the kids who, through no fault of their own, had their lives predetermined by their environments. These were the ones who, despite having the intelligence, aptitude, and drive, were fated to succumb to the crushing weight of circumstance. They lived in neglected communities rife with gang violence, substance abuse, and the ever-present specter of generational poverty. The deck was stacked against them from the moment they drew their first breath. Their families were fractured, their homes were unsafe, and the odds of escaping their predicament seemed infinitesimally small. They faced constant setbacks, a relentless stream of disappointments that chipped away at their hope and eroded their dreams.   I also felt for those who struggled with mental health issues. The pressures of adolescence, coupled with the anxieties of navigating a complex and often unforgiving world, could be agonizing. They grappled with depression, social awkwardness, or overwhelming feelings of inadequacy. The school system offered scant support for these students, viewing them as inconvenient distractions. Their pains were frequently dismissed or misunderstood by peers and even by adults. They often suffered in silence, their struggles hidden behind facades of normalcy or outward displays of rebellion. It's a tragedy how many of them never got the help that they desperately needed and deserved. Sometimes, I would imagine how their lives would turn out when they became adults.

Which supporting actress was much more memorable than the star of a movie? I'm going to say Anne Heche in *Six Days, Seven Nights* (1998). Harrison Ford, the star, was his usual stoic self, but Anne Heche was, well, Anne Heche. You know what I mean? The movie, a rom-com action-adventure flick, saw her as a New Yorker magazine editor stranded on a remote island in the South Pacific with a grumpy pilot (Ford). It was Heche who brought the real energy, quirkiness, and genuine warmth of the film, especially with the backdrop of the film’s scenery and the chemistry between them. Heche's performance was so vibrant that it overshadowed Ford's more understated contribution. It's a testament to her acting prowess that even alongside a Hollywood titan, she managed to steal the show, not just in terms of screen time, but in the audience's hearts. Ford played the role well, but let’s be honest: how many people genuinely remember his role? It's Heche's performance that has endured in the memories of those who have seen the film. Maybe it's because her role was so different from her usual roles. It was an explosion of personality which was a departure from her roles in movies like *Donnie Brasco* and *Wag the Dog*. She brought a comedic timing to the movie that lifted its overall appeal to new heights, and she was gorgeous, too. She was also able to act as a credible romantic lead, and her character's transformation from a stressed-out city girl to a resourceful survivor was compelling, relatable, and utterly entertaining. She captured the audience’s attention. The film may have been a hit, but it's Heche's performance that lingers long after the credits roll, making her, for me, far more memorable than the star. And it's always a nice touch when the support wins the game.

What is the scariest moment you have had in your own home? Growing up in a household where violence was a regular occurrence, there were certainly many moments of unadulterated terror. But I'd have to say one evening lingers most vividly in my memory. Our house was a modest two-story dwelling, situated on a quiet, dimly lit cul-de-sac. My parents, bless their souls, were out for the evening, leaving my younger siblings and me under the watchful eye of a teenage babysitter. We were all in our rooms, ostensibly doing homework, though I, being the eldest, was more likely lost in the pages of a sci-fi novel, my younger siblings engaged in a rather boisterous game of hide-and-seek.  The clock struck 1 AM, and I decided to get a glass of water from the kitchen. As I descended the stairs, I could hear a faint, rhythmic thumping emanating from outside. I peered through the peephole of the front door and saw nothing. This was not that uncommon as our house was flanked by a thicket of trees and bushes. I unlocked the door to see if I could discern anything. The thumping was getting louder, and now I realized it was a low, guttural animal sound. Slowly, cautiously, I pushed the door wider and looked around, the light of the porch illuminating the darkness. A pair of gleaming red eyes stared back at me from the shadows of the thicket, a large dog, its teeth bared in what I perceived was a menacing, aggressive snarl. It was no ordinary dog, however. It was a massive specimen, its fur matted with dirt and leaves. One of my siblings let out a scream, a sound that instantly petrified me. My feet were frozen where I stood. The dog seemed to sense my fear, its low growl intensifying. I slammed the door shut, my heart pounding in my chest. We never truly felt secure in our home after that night.

Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? There are many. However, I'll confine myself to providing some examples of actors who by and large are not considered A-listers, but delivered standout performances due to roles that were exceptionally well-written. These roles, in turn, showcased their inherent abilities to a degree that might have otherwise remained hidden. Take, for instance, the character of Lester Burnham in *American Beauty* (1999). Kevin Spacey, already a highly-regarded actor at the time, delivered a nuanced and powerful performance that transcended the expected narrative. But across his career, Spacey has often been in big budget affairs that didn't allow him to breathe life deeply into his characters. Burnham, on the other hand, was a complex, flawed man grappling with a mid-life crisis. The brilliance of the writing, coupled with Spacey's talent, created a character that was both repulsive and sympathetic. Similarly, consider William H. Macy in *Fargo* (1996). Macy is a reliable, dependable character actor but could have been considered average prior to this role. Jerry Lundegaard, the hapless car salesman was a masterpiece of characterization; his desperate attempts to overcome bad decisions painted a portrait of desperation. Macy took the material and ran with it. Another excellent example is John C. Reilly as Detective Jim Kurring in *Boogie Nights* (1997). Reilly is an actor. But Kurring became a beloved character and is almost certainly what would spring to a viewer’s mind when his name came up - I doubt many other roles have achieved that level of recognition. He gave a performance of such raw emotional honesty that elevated the film. Finally, let’s not forget the quiet brilliance of Steve Buscemi as Mr. Pink in *Reservoir Dogs* (1992). Buscemi is no Cary Grant, but could not have been any other individual as Mr. Pink. The character's cynical pragmatism and underlying vulnerability were brought to life through the skillful dialogue and Buscemi's understated delivery, cementing him as the perfect actor for the role. The quality of these performances highlights the symbiotic relationship between skilled writing and accomplished acting and how the combination of both can create moments that continue to resonate long after the credits roll.

Have you ever had a co-worker who you worked closely with get fired for something truly shocking that you never saw coming? As a rule, the workplace is a peculiar ecosystem. You spend at least 8 hours a day, five days a week, perhaps even more, with people you may or may not have a rapport with. You build friendships with colleagues and can also find yourself in situations of begrudging tolerance with others. I've always found it fascinating how a workplace can sometimes feel like a slightly more structured version of high school, complete with cliques, gossip, and the inevitable power dynamics. I had an experience a few years ago that, even now, I find myself revisiting from time to time. Let me set the scene. I worked in the IT department of a well-established accounting firm in Port of Spain. We were a small team: myself, the IT manager, and two other technicians. One of the technicians, let's call him Mark, was a real character. He was the archetypal ‘tech guy’—always buried in code, a man who, even on a casual Friday, seemed most comfortable in a t-shirt emblazoned with some obscure programming language and a pair of worn jeans. He was also, to put it mildly, eccentric. His desk was an indescribable mess of wires, half-eaten takeout containers, and assorted tech gadgets. Despite his quirks, Mark was incredibly knowledgeable and a damn good technician, capable of troubleshooting almost any IT issue. I genuinely liked the guy so when he got fired for ‘misappropriation of company resources’ I nearly fell out of my chair. We had been friends at work and would share everything, from our favourite movies to our latest dating woes. Misappropriation was a serious charge! It was a term usually related to embezzlement or theft of goods on a massive scale. As I got into the office that day, a colleague, Sarah, beckoned me aside. ‘Have you heard?’ she asked, eyes wide with a mixture of shock and glee. I shook my head, already sensing something wrong. Sarah, bless her heart, was never the best keeper of secrets so she blurted out the news. Mark had been fired. The whispers around the office were that he was fired for stealing.

If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? This question immediately conjures images of epic fantasy, doesn't it? While the mind races with possibilities, a few stand out. The lion, with its sheer presence and primal roar, would be a terrifying mount. Imagine the battlefield, the dust swirling, and the thunderous advance of a horse-sized lion, a mane of fury, leading the charge. That's a fearsome sight, indeed. Conversely, a giant, battle-ready elephant, a war beast of the ancient times, thundering across the battlefield, crushing all in its path, is another image that pops up in the mind. However, for me, a horse-sized falcon is the most majestic to ride into battle. The ability to soar above the fray, survey the battlefield with its piercing gaze, and swoop down with the speed of a bullet, is a tactical advantage that transcends the brute force of a lion or the lumbering power of elephants. Furthermore, the falcon embodies agility, freedom, and a certain elegant danger: the perfect combination for the ultimate battlefield mount. It doesn't have the brute strength of others but its control of the skies and its breathtaking speed makes it a fearsome beast to behold. One imagines a rider on a horse-sized falcon: a knight in shining armour, with a sword drawn, atop a gargantuan bird of prey. The sun glinting off its feathers as it dives towards the enemy. A sight that will freeze the hearts of your enemies through sheer fear. Edit: I forgot to include that the horse-sized falcon will be a significant pain to feed.

What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? I once witnessed a woman, and I'm using the term woman loosely here, deliberately open a box of expensive assorted chocolates, gorge herself on half of them, and then casually return the mangled container to the shelf. No attempt at stealth. No furtive glances. Just a brazen display of entitlement and a complete disregard for the next customer. It wasn't the act itself, although that was pretty revolting, but the utter lack of shame that really got to me. She strolled through the aisle, a trail of half-eaten chocolate in her wake, radiating a sense of smug indifference. It was as if she believed the grocery store was there solely for her amusement, and the concept of paying for anything was a quaint suggestion. To add insult to injury, she was yammering away on her phone the entire time, oblivious to the disapproving stares of everyone around her. I wanted to confront her, to berate her, to make her at least slightly cognizant of her appalling behavior, but I was frozen with disbelief. I mean, who does that? It was truly a master class in public idiocy.

What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? I'm not much of a fan of the corporate world, let alone the benefits they offer, so you can imagine my reaction to the incentives I've encountered over the years. My first job, a summer gig at a local supermarket, offered a "discounted employee meal" at the deli counter - a measly 10% off, mind you, on items already priced with a healthy markup. Not exactly a perk to write home about, and hardly enough compensation for enduring the endless tedium of stocking shelves. My second job at a call center. We received "employee of the month" awards. The award itself was a certificate and a dedicated parking spot that was always in the sun. Then there’s the wellness programs; the ones that offer "free" gym memberships and meditation sessions. One company I worked for made a big deal about their on-site gym. It was tucked away in a windowless basement, equipped with a couple of dusty treadmills and a weight machine that looked older than I was. The worst perk came from a tech startup that I interviewed with. The recruiter started going on about the "collaborative" office space, described how we would be encouraged to "think outside the box." The interviewer then pulled out a brochure and described the "Unlimited vacation time" policy, which sounds awesome until you realize it comes with the unspoken expectation that you’d feel guilty for taking any time off. They also gave out 'free' beer on Fridays because of the 'tech culture'. I didn't get the job. But the most lamentable "benefit" I ever encountered came from a job I actually took. It involved working in a back office for a bank - a job as uninspiring as it sounds.

What is your 10-year gap photo? This is a very interesting question, and I must confess, it spurred a wave of introspection. Ten years. A decade. It feels like a blink of an eye, and yet, a lifetime’s worth of experiences, growth, and metamorphosis has occurred. To capture this in a single image, a static photograph? It's insufficient. My ten-year gap photo isn't a singular snapshot; it’s a collage, a mosaic of moments, triumphs, and, yes, even failures. The backdrop in 2014 held a vibrant energy: freshly graduated with an IT degree, an overflowing sense of optimism, and a world stretched out before me, ripe with opportunity. I was brimming with ambitions, envisioning startups, international travel and of course the conquest of the written word. My beard was shorter, my hair was less grey. I probably still didn't know how to cook anything beyond boiling water for pasta. Fast forward to 2024, and the skyline has shifted. The landscape feels less stark; the challenges seem more textured, more nuanced. The sharp angles have softened, the relentless ambition tempered but certainly not vanished. There are responsibilities, and an understanding of the world I did not have a decade before. Yet both photos share a single thread: a relentless sense of curiosity.

At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? I’m not certain I ever truly enjoyed YA fiction. Sure, I read the occasional book in my teens, mostly out of obligation. My friends were reading it, it was the cultural zeitgeist, and I didn't want to be left out. But even then, I often found myself rolling my eyes at the predictable tropes, the overwrought melodrama, and the simplistic moral lessons. Perhaps that's a bit harsh, but the truth is, the majority of the books I encountered in the genre felt… juvenile. I was always searching for something with a bit more substance, more complexity, something that actually challenged me. The same way with the music or movies I consumed. I understood its mass appeal, of course. YA fiction provided a safe, accessible space for young readers to explore complex issues, come to terms with the confusing emotions of adolescence, and dream of escaping their mundane realities. But I was reading, and looking for books that did the same, but with more depth. I suppose I was looking for that same escape, just through literature of a higher order.

Who is the best classic rock drummer? No discussion is complete without mentioning the names of the Gods of Rock drumming, so let’s get that ceremonial business out of the way upfront: John Bonham, Keith Moon, and Neil Peart. To omit any of these three is to signal one’s ignorance, or to come across as just being plain contrarian. All three were virtuosos who, besides having a powerful grip on the fundamentals of drumming such as timing and tempo, all had a knack for inventive, awe-inspiring performances. Bonham was the hard-hitting powerhouse, the brute force of rhythm driving Led Zeppelin’s thunderous sound. Moon, the flamboyant, unpredictable showman, whose manic energy defined The Who’s controlled chaos. Peart, the cerebral craftsman, who brought a melodic sensibility to Rush’s progressive rock. However, when it comes to the question of the ‘best’ classic rock drummer, it doesn't end there, even when considering those giants that define the genre. It's essential to recognize that one's preference often boils down to personal taste as there were so many other talented musicians to choose from. Ringo Starr was a man who often went unrecognized for his talents. He was the glue that held the Beatles together rhythmically. His simple fills and solid backbeats provided the perfect foundation for Lennon and McCartney’s songwriting genius to shine through. There's also Ginger Baker, a flamboyant jazz and Afrobeat influenced pioneer who helped shape the sound of Cream, one of the most influential bands of the late 60's. Then there's also Charlie Watts whose drumming provided a subtle backbone for The Rolling Stones.

Why are so many men scared to date single mothers? There is this somewhat illogical argument, a trope actually, that single mothers are somehow damaged goods - battered, weathered, and broken by life and love. That somehow they’re “used” or “worn out.” As though women are cars and men are mechanics. As a man, I find this train of thought not just offensive but utterly preposterous. Firstly, the fact that a woman has been in a previous relationship, even had children, doesn’t diminish her value. It simply means she's experienced life, perhaps learned some lessons, and has grown. And let's be clear; she’s likely endured more hardships than the average man. Raising a child, often alone, is no easy feat. Secondly, the implication that all single mothers are somehow damaged goods, or that they are all equally difficult to be with is, frankly, insulting. Some single mothers may indeed have baggage. Many of them might even come with drama and trauma. But so do *all* people, regardless of their marital status or parental situation! Each individual has a different set of experiences that form them as a person. Some of them will bring a positive or challenging outlook on life. A potential partner should be assessed by their virtues and their faults, separately, as a matter of course. To dismiss someone based on a stereotype is lazy and intellectually dishonest. Thirdly, let’s address the elephant in the room: children. Some men express fear of being a father figure to someone else’s kids. This is reasonable. The adjustment is not always easy. But if you are not ready to act as a parent to the children, you shouldn’t even bother with the mother. Some men are intimidated by the sense of responsibility, the financial burden, and the emotional investment that comes with being in a relationship with women. So, they avoid single mothers, believing it is twice as much work and effort. But as they say, "no guts, no glory." There are many advantages to dating a single mother: she is often more mature, more independent, and less likely to engage in silly games. She has already gone through a lot. She probably has her priorities straight. She has no time for mediocrity. She can teach you a lot about responsibility and love. Plus, you get to benefit from all her lessons. Her lessons. If a man is scared to date a single mother they need to ask themselves the tough questions. It's not a matter of the single mother being damaged or problematic. Quite the contrary. The very act of being frightened shows that *that* man is the damaged party.

What is the biggest lie society has taught you to believe? That hard work guarantees success. I understand where this belief comes from. It makes sense that it's been propagated in the Western world, particularly in the countries that broke away from various forms of monarchy and feudalism several centuries ago. In the old system, your bloodline and connections decided your place in society and how much wealth you could accumulate. Hard work was only useful if you were born of the right parentage. In the new society, the story goes, anyone could be whatever they wanted if they but put in the effort. The problem is that this is a fallacy. If the statement were true, then we would be living in a meritocracy, and that is simply not what we have. We are not allowed to talk of class in polite company, but it is ever present in our lives. It's perfectly fine to be born into wealth. It is also perfectly fine to be a trust-fund baby, to have your parents pay your way through college, to get your first house and job and a thousand other advantages that can be found in being born into the right social class. However, if you are not born into wealth, then you would be a fool to not work hard but work hard is only one small aspect of ‘success.’ Success is hard work, a degree of good luck, who you know (your network), economic conditions, race, gender, family background, geography, etc. There are times where I have put in 60 hours a week and barely got noticed. There are other times where I have done next to nothing and received accolades and reward. The difference: timing and who was looking. I would have been better served and have been better served in the past, by learning to network my way through life, rather than working hard. More importantly, I would have been far better off if I had been born in the correct class. It would have guaranteed comfort, perhaps success. The biggest lie society has taught me: Anyone can be whatever he wants if they work hard. The evidence shows that this is plainly incorrect.

Were you popular in high school? I was a good student, in the advanced classes, and always made an effort to be affable to most people - so I wouldn’t say I was unpopular. However, I wasn’t what you would call popular in high school. That’s important to clarify - because there are different connotations of what constitutes a ‘popular’ person in high school. The jocks, cheerleaders, those who were physically attractive, came from wealthy families, and had a high social media presence are easily identifiable as popular people. They are usually the ones at the head of all school activities. I wasn’t one of them. But I wasn’t picked on or bullied. I had friends, I had pleasant interactions with the majority of people, but I certainly wasn’t invited to parties, didn’t go on dates, and never had a girlfriend or a group of girls fighting for my affections. My friends and I existed in a sort of self-imposed social bubble, and we were perfectly fine with this. We didn't care for the theatrics and superficiality of the ‘in’ crowd. If anything, we were quite disdainful of them. We would watch them with a sort of anthropological interest, studying their behaviour like creatures in a zoo. We had our own inside jokes, shared interests in nerdish activities such as video games, fantasy novels, and obscure movies. Now, it's all well and good to say that I was indifferent and didn't care for all the 'high school' stuff but, of course, that’s revisionist history. In the moment, you don't understand. Most teenagers have no life experience to draw upon and simply have to go through the motions. We weren’t privy to great wisdom at the time. It’s only in the benefit of hindsight that I can appreciate the value of those years. One can always appreciate the value of a period of time when one does not have responsibilities or debts, when one's only concern is doing well in school and being generally a decent human being. That said, I won't lie. I did feel inadequate at times, especially when a classmate would get a girlfriend or a boyfriend and then rub the relationship in everyone's face. The feelings are not as severe now, but I remember them. I would not say I'm thankful for these feelings because they had an impact on my personality. Now at my age I don’t care all that much about the feelings I once had. They are there to be explored, understood – perhaps even used as fuel for some creative endeavour. However, to answer the question as succinctly as possible: I was not popular. And I am more than fine with that.

What are some inaccuracies or criticisms of JD Vance's book "Hillbilly Elegy"? J.D. Vance’s *Hillbilly Elegy* has garnered significant attention, both positive and negative, since its publication. The inaccuracies are numerous, and the criticisms, varied. One common point of contention centers on Vance's portrayal of Appalachian culture and the economic realities of the region. Critics argue that his account simplifies the complexities of poverty, addiction, and social dysfunction within the Appalachian community. His focus on personal responsibility, while not entirely unwarranted, downplays the systemic issues such as the decline of manufacturing jobs and the lack of economic opportunities that have plagued the region for decades. Furthermore, some scholars and individuals from the region itself have questioned the authenticity of Vance's narrative, suggesting that his experiences are not universally representative of the hillbilly experience. The book's romanticization of certain cultural aspects, particularly a perceived toughness and resilience, is seen by some as a distortion, a cherry-picking of particular aspects of Appalachian life out of context, as well as a misrepresentation of the challenges his community face. Moreover, Vance has been criticized for generalizing and stereotyping, often portraying all those in his community as sharing the same values on a myriad of issues. His conservative political views, and the book's subsequent reception within conservative circles, led to accusations that he uses his memoir to justify particular political stances and promote specific policy solutions. Many critics of the book, while not dismissing all of Vance's observations, contend that *Hillbilly Elegy* offers an incomplete and sometimes misleading picture of a multifaceted community, overlooking institutional and historical factors. It is, in short, a flawed piece of work, at best.

What's the most obnoxious instance of America-centric behavior you've ever witnessed? My first job in media was working for a small publishing house in Trinidad. The company mostly produced government-funded pamphlets on healthcare, agriculture, and infrastructure. They had a small, but growing, international outreach, and were desperately trying to get their hands on a lucrative English-language publication deal in the United States. The American executives were condescending and arrogant. The negotiations were going nowhere. They were shocked that we hadn't heard of their obscure publishing house that specialized in pamphlets about ‘the correct way to fold a flag.’ They were mystified that we used the Queen’s English and not American English and kept asking us if we could change our ‘funny’ language to theirs. Their biggest complaint was that our pamphlets were too ‘wordy,’ an insult to the very core of the English language and any writing based upon it. I had had it with their nonsense when I was tasked with hosting one of those executives who was visiting our office. I was told to ‘make him feel comfortable.’ He arrived with a baseball cap, an American flag t-shirt and a can of soda (which by the way, he loudly pronounced as ‘soder’). Throughout the day he kept asking me if I was able to watch American football and baseball and if I knew who the president of the United States was. It was as if this was the only thing of value I needed to know to be considered a human being. Then he expressed disappointment that Port of Spain, our capital, had no strip malls, baseball stadiums, or Walmart. Later on he was confused as to why none of us had ever heard of the popular American sitcom ‘Seinfeld’. He asked in an incredulous tone, “You all *still* haven’t seen Seinfeld?!?” I decided to play along. “No, we have never heard of it.” “Oh. Well, in that case I apologize. I was under the impression every single person in the entire world watches it all the time,” he responded, with utter conviction. “I understand,” I replied. “We generally assume that every single person in the world speaks the same dialect of French as you. It is a bit of a shock when we realize that others simply don’t.” He just stared at me blankly. Then he asked what I was talking about. I just shrugged. Another time, I was visiting a friend who was doing his Masters in New York. I was sitting in a coffee shop reading a book when I overheard a conversation between two American university students. “I still can’t understand why people choose to live outside America. I mean, what else is there?” one of them said. “I know, right? How are people who don’t live in America even happy?” the other one responded. I thought the lack of self-awareness was breathtaking. I really wanted to interject, but held my tongue. The next day I was riding the subway. A woman saw my passport. “Oh, you're from Trinidad and Tobago! That's so cool, I've always wanted to visit the Bahamas,” she gushed. I resisted the urge to correct her.

What are some of the biggest casting blunders in Hollywood movies? There have been many, but three, in particular, come to mind. The first, and probably the most egregious, is the casting of Mickey Rooney as the Japanese character Mr. Yunioshi in *Breakfast at Tiffany's*. This was a gross caricature, laden with offensive stereotypes, and remains one of the most embarrassing moments in Hollywood history. The second is the relatively recent casting of white actors to portray Middle Eastern characters. This egregious practice is particularly prevalent in action films from the 1980s. The third is the practice of casting actors who don't fit the physical description or age range of the character they are playing. While this sometimes works, most times it doesn’t. A prime example of casting an actor so that it ends up becoming a blunder is the casting of Tom Cruise as Jack Reacher. Reacher is a hulking six-foot-five mountain of a man, while Cruise is…well, not. I’m not saying that an actor cannot embody or successfully portray any character outside of their own physical and inherent attributes. But given the character's inherent physical attributes, this was always going to be a tough ask. The whole enterprise falls flat for those who have read the books. What's worse is that both films were not great. No one is blaming Cruise for that. Cruise gives it his all. The blame belongs to who created a sub-par film that was never true to the source material. A good director will have a vision or a unique take on a film. A great director will also have a thorough respect for the source material and what it is about. Sometimes a terrible performance, a bad casting, or a poor screenplay can sink even the most promising movie. But sometimes a bad movie happens because certain ingredients are not given the right amount of attention. The most famous and best example of all of this is the disastrous *John Carter*.

What's the dumbest thing you've gotten in trouble for at school? In high school, I was a fairly good student. I was always on the Dean's list, active in debate, and generally stayed out of trouble. However, I did have one notable instance of crossing the line that came back to haunt me. My school had a strict no-hat policy. We were not allowed to wear hats, caps, beanies, any head covering whatsoever, inside the building including during lunchtime in the cafeteria. One day, I strolled into the cafeteria with a brand new, very stylish, black fedora. I sat with my friends, we ate our lunch and had a jolly time. I completely forgot about the hat. Boom! The next day, I was summoned to the principal's office. I don't remember what the official punishment was. What I do remember is the principal giving me a severe lecture and threatening to suspend me. It was completely absurd and a watershed moment of realising that my actions can sometimes be punished according to a certain arbitrary standard.

Who won the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden? It's difficult to definitively say who 'won' the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden, as the measure of victory is intensely subjective and dependent on the individual observer's biases and preconceived notions. Media outlets, political analysts, and social media users all offered their own assessments, often colored by their political leanings. Some focused on the candidates' specific policy proposals, while others homed in on their perceived demeanor, speaking style, or the effectiveness of their attacks. Ultimately, the 'winner' of any debate is often determined by public opinion and its subsequent impact on voter perception and, of course, the polls. Both candidates likely had moments where they appeared to score points, land a punch, or appear to have stumbled. It is almost a certainty, however, that both candidates would have supporters and detractors in each camp.

What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? The common parenting mistake, in my estimation, is an unwillingness to acknowledge the distinct individuality of each child. Parents, in their well-intentioned efforts to guide and nurture, often fall into the trap of applying a one-size-fits-all approach, failing to recognize that children are not cookie-cutter versions of themselves, nor are they simply reflections of the parents' own aspirations. This manifests in various forms, whether it’s pushing a child into a specific academic path, ignoring their artistic inclinations, or comparing them unfavorably to siblings or peers. I've observed this firsthand in my own upbringing, the subtle pressures to conform to expectations that didn't necessarily align with my own interests or strengths. Ironically, this sort of parenting can also manifest itself in a child's insistence to always strive for perfection. The remedy for this lies in a shift in perspective. Parents must cultivate a keen sense of observation, carefully watching and listening to their children to discern what truly motivates and excites them. It's about fostering an environment where children feel safe to explore their own identities, to stumble and learn from their mistakes without fear of judgment. It requires a willingness to adapt, to adjust expectations and parenting strategies to suit the specific needs of each child. This means celebrating individual talents, supporting passions, and accepting that success may look different for each child. Moreover, it's critical for parents to acknowledge their own biases, to reflect on their own experiences and how these might be unconsciously influencing their parenting choices. The goal isn't just to raise successful individuals, but to nurture well-rounded, self-assured human beings who are free to forge their own paths and embrace their unique potential.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? I possess no statistical data to definitively assert that Europe is more, less, or comparably racist to the USA. However, I can proffer observations. I've lived in the United States for an extended period, worked in predominantly white-collar industries, and travelled extensively throughout Europe, mostly for leisure. The racial dynamics of the two continents appear distinct, rooted in varying histories and societal structures. The USA, grappling with its legacy of slavery and segregation, often exhibits a more overt, confrontational form of racism. One might argue that it is more "in your face." Conversely, Europe, while lacking America's overt history of legalized slavery, presents a more subtle form, frequently manifested in institutional biases and prejudiced attitudes towards immigrants and minority groups, particularly those of non-European descent. I've seen instances of racism, albeit expressed differently, in both contexts. It’s seldom as simple as "Europe is more racist." Racism in Europe is often intertwined with xenophobia, particularly in the realm of immigration. The rise of right-wing populist movements across the continent reveals a deep-seated fear of the "other," a sentiment that is often couched in terms of cultural preservation which ultimately, is a fancy word for racism. Furthermore, the historical context is paramount. The USA's history is directly tied to the enslavement of Africans and the subjugation of Native Americans. Europe’s colonial past created the economic exploitation of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. The consequences of these historical transgressions continue to reverberate to this day. The racism prevalent in the present day arises from historical and cultural contexts, and one’s experiences may vary. The USA's treatment of its citizens, while improved, can be appalling. Likewise, so too can the attitudes and behaviours of the Europeans to the minorities among them.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? This is a difficult question to answer, as “underestimated” is a subjective term. But for me, a strong candidate for the most underestimated horror movie villain is Howard, the seemingly unassuming neighbor in *10 Cloverfield Lane*. Mary Elizabeth Winstead's character, Michelle, is abducted and held prisoner in Howard's underground bunker. Initially, he presents himself as a concerned, possibly even heroic, figure protecting her from an outside threat – an alien invasion. John Goodman’s portrayal of Howard is a masterclass in building tension. He oozes a folksy charm that masks a dark undercurrent. He controls the narrative; it is all through his point of view that Michelle assesses the situation. He is a manipulative, obsessive individual. He is a survivalist, an apparent patriot. But, as the film progresses, it becomes increasingly clear that Howard is the real monster, and his version of reality – his rules, his control – is far more dangerous than any perceived external threat. The true horror comes from his capacity for violence, his twisted sense of justice, and his complete lack of empathy. He’s the embodiment of the phrase, “the devil you know.” This is a villain who wields psychological manipulation and physical intimidation expertly, making him a far more potent threat than any rampaging creature or masked slasher. He doesn't need supernatural powers or elaborate weaponry; his control over his environment and the vulnerability of his captives makes him a truly terrifying antagonist: He is the kind of villain who makes you question not just the safety of his victims, but also the very nature of trust.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? One random school day, I was around eight years old, I had a massive nosebleed. Not a minor one that stopped after a few tissues; this was a full-on, cinematic eruption. Blood was gushing from my nostrils like a geyser, staining my school uniform and the unfortunate desk in front of me. The teacher, a stern but fair woman, rushed me to the school nurse’s office. However, the nurse, a rather portly lady, seemed more flustered than concerned. After haphazardly stuffing cotton wool up my nose, she unceremoniously informed me that I was a lost cause and advised my teacher to call my mother, who was, at the time, as reliable as a chocolate teapot. My mother would undoubtedly have been at work and unavailable for hours. Any parent knows that the school system is a well-oiled machine designed to ensure that you can never get away with your shift-work schedule. The school principal, a tall, imposing figure with a disapproving glare, was summoned. He surveyed the scene: a distressed child, a desk resembling a crime scene, and a flustered nurse. He sighed dramatically, as if I were personally inconveniencing his day. Just as I was steeling myself for the inevitable scolding, a quiet voice spoke up. It was my classmate, a shy, unassuming boy named Rohan, who was never usually one for sticking his neck out. Rohan came to me to help. I had never known Rohan to have any courage; He was typically at the back of the class. But here he was. He spoke to the principal, who regarded him with barely concealed displeasure. “Sir, my mother works nearby. She can come.” The principal, visibly irritated, waved his hand dismissively. “Fine, fine." He probably thought he was ridding himself of the issue. Rohan turned to me, his face a mixture of concern and determination. He told me he would come with me. I wasn’t keen but at that point I wasn’t in a position to argue. Rohan took my hand, and led me out of the office and onto the school compound where he had his cousin waiting and the both of us walked hand in hand to his mother’s workplace. Rohan’s mother, a kind-faced woman with gentle eyes, took one look at me and immediately calmed me. She cleaned me up, got me a change of clothes, and, even more unbelievably, stayed with me until my aunt (who lived closer to the school), arrived some two hours later. She was patient and reassuring, qualities sadly lacking in the adults at the school. That day, Rohan, a quiet, unremarkable boy, became a hero. It wasn't a grand gesture or a dramatic rescue; it was the simple act of compassion and kindness from a peer that made all the difference, a reminder that even in the most chaotic moments, there is always someone willing to lend a helping hand.
