The memory of Rohan's kindness stayed with me, a powerful antidote to the cynicism that often pervades the world, proof that even at the tender age of eight, the smallest acts can have the greatest impact.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? Ah, the eternal struggle, right? The awkward dance of professional self-identification. I get it. The janitorial arts, while vital, don’t exactly elicit awe at cocktail parties. Let's finesse this. You could lean into the "facility maintenance" angle – it sounds more corporate, more… important. Or, if you want to get a bit more specific, try "building services specialist." That hints at a broader skill set, a mastery of the physical environment. "Environmental services technician" rolls off the tongue nicely, even if it's a bit of a reach. If you work mostly with the operational aspects of the school, "operations specialist" is also a viable option. If these don’t quite fit the bill, consider this little gem: "I'm the guy who keeps the wheels turning." It's broad, intriguing, and suggests a degree of indispensable responsibility. Of course, if you feel particularly cheeky, "I'm a sanitation engineer" will get a laugh, though that might elicit follow-up questions you'd rather avoid. The key is to find a phrase that projects confidence and suggests a certain level of expertise, even if that expertise involves wrestling with overflowing bins and battling the forces of crayon-wielding toddlers. Ultimately, the words are less important than the inflection. Say it with pride, a twinkle in your eye, and you can even make ‘custodian’ sound rather glamorous.

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? Having competed and lost more times than I care to remember, I can attest to the potent sting of the "almost." Silver medalists, it seems, are far more prone to the mental gymnastics of "what ifs" — the counterfactual thinking. They dwell on the tantalizing nearness of victory, replaying the moments that slipped through their grasp. "If only I’d pushed harder on that last lap!" they lament. "If I hadn't stumbled at that crucial moment!" Their minds are a relentless reel of near misses and could-have-beens. The bronze medalist, on the other hand, is more likely to experience a surge of relief. They narrowly escaped the ignominy of no medal at all. For them, the counterfactual is, "At least I didn't come in fourth!" The bronze is a triumph over the vast majority who didn't even make the podium. This is a phenomenon easily relatable off the athletic field. Think of a job interview. You are one of many candidates. You are in the final two. The other candidate is offered the job. You do not get the job. If you dwell on the fact you were one of two, if not the one chosen, you would be in a state of dejection far more profound than the candidate who didn't make the final cut but was never even considered, and can only imagine what was. The same goes for purchasing a car: after weeks of researching and test drives, you finally settle on one but as the paperwork is being processed, the car is sold out from under you. You would be a lot more upset than the person who never got on the lot, but only dreamed of someday purchasing that car. It's a curious paradox of the human psyche: Near misses often hurt more than outright failures.

What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? Before I get into this, I'd like to confess that I've never been a con artist. I'm usually the sucker. But I know a con when I see one. So I was sitting at a bar in downtown Port-of-Spain. The place was packed, the music was loud, everybody was having a good time. A guy approached me, seemingly out of nowhere. He was an older gentleman, well-dressed, sporting a neatly trimmed white beard, and radiating a genuine warmth. He introduced himself as "David," and after a short conversation, he expressed his interest in my watch, a relatively inexpensive Timex I'd had for years. "Nice watch, sir," he said. "You know, I'm a bit of a collector. I would be willing to pay you a good sum for it." I was taken aback; the watch wasn't worth much, but the proposition was flattering. I played it cool, pretending I didn't immediately grasp the situation. This wasn't a robbery; he was offering to *buy* it. I asked him how much.  "Let's not haggle," David said, "I'll give you two hundred dollars for it."  I should have smelled a rat. I knew that the watch was not, under any stretch of the imagination, worth anywhere near that amount. But here's where I went wrong: the offer was made in front of the whole bar. The guy had an air of respectability and was using a technique that I didn't know then but I know now. David seemed to be suggesting some sort of business deal, not some back alley transaction. I was not sure how to negotiate in front of a crowded bar. My guard was lowered, and I was momentarily captivated by the illusion of a windfall. I played along. I pulled the watch from my wrist, fully intending to say something like, "Okay sure, if it's no bother", then laugh and say "just kidding". I made a show of hesitating. "Well...," I began, feigning reluctance, "It was my father's.." He cut me off. "Here." He pulled two crisp hundred dollar bills from his wallet. "It's a deal?"  I took the money with a grin and almost immediately recognized I'd just been scammed when he walked away from the bar with his prize, heading toward the front door. I watched him with a mixture of bewilderment and amusement. I looked down at my empty wrist - I did not even have a wrist watch anymore. The whole thing felt so bizarre that I almost couldn't be angry. I considered chasing after him, demanding the watch back or at least a more accurate price, but the whole thing was just too silly. No matter how hard I tried, I couldn't convince myself to ruin the mood of a lively night at a packed bar. I decided to let it go. I finished my drink, shook my head, and chuckled at my naiveté. The truth is, I'd been hustled, bamboozled, and hoodwinked. But the con was so elegantly executed, and the payout so relatively small, that I couldn't help but admire the man's skill; two hundred dollars for one cheap Timex. It was a masterstroke of deceptive simplicity.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? Hollywood’s portrayal of the U.S., like any cinematic rendition of a complex reality, is often a distorted mirror, reflecting back a refracted image of the nation. It's a funhouse mirror at times, exaggerating certain features while obscuring others. One enduring trope is the glorification of American exceptionalism, where the U.S. is depicted as the perpetual savior of the world, swooping in to rescue humanity from any and every conceivable threat. This is a constant, whether it's battling alien invaders, thwarting global terrorist plots, or simply solving the trivial problems of some obscure, far-flung nation. This overplayed narrative often neglects the messy realities of international relations, depicting other countries and cultures as either threats or beneficiaries, with little nuance in between.  Another common misrepresentation is the romanticized and often sanitized depiction of American history. Historical events are regularly simplified, often ignoring the darker chapters of its past. Difficult topics such as slavery, the treatment of Native Americans, and the complexities of the Civil Rights movement are often glossed over, or presented in a way that downplays their severity. The focus is often on the ‘triumphant’ narrative, highlighting the nation’s progress while conveniently eliding the struggles of those who were marginalized or disenfranchised. Hollywood also loves to showcase the opulence and glamour of American life, giving viewers around the world a glimpse into a world of sprawling mansions, designer clothes, and fast cars. While this may reflect a portion of American society, it does not portray the everyday lives of the average American. Most Americans live paycheck to paycheck. This leads to unrealistic expectations and reinforces the perception of a country where everyone is rich and successful.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? It's a tie, for me, between Barry Lyndon (1975) and 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968). Stanley Kubrick has an uncanny ability to make you feel not only like a participant in the drama before your eyes but as an observer, a voyeur, a fly on the wall. In Barry Lyndon, the natural lighting from candles and the slow, deliberate pace make you feel like you are right there in the 18th century. Likewise, 2001: A Space Odyssey’s long, lingering shots of outer space, the almost complete absence of dialogue, and the eerie, disorienting score make you feel like you yourself are floating through the cosmos. I'm certain that both of these movies, regardless of how many times I re-watch them, will never cease to invoke that feeling of complete immersion. They’re the cinematic equivalent of stepping inside a dream. My honorable mention, however, goes to the much more accessible Lawrence of Arabia (1962). The vast, sweeping shots of the desert, the stirring score, and the epic scope of the story make you feel as if you are riding alongside Peter O’Toole as he leads his Arab army to victory. Also, that score by Maurice Jarre gives me goosebumps every time I watch the movie.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? I cannot say much about what goes on in the kitchen – having never worked at a fast food restaurant – but I do have some theories regarding the marketing that I’ve observed over the years. The first that comes to mind (and this isn’t all that surprising for many people, I grant you) is the ‘perpetual discount’ scam. It is the easiest trick in the book. McDonald’s is perhaps the biggest offender but almost every fast food chain will do this at any given time. You will see items advertised at “discounted” prices. Prices that are purportedly lower than usual. However, it is all a sham. Those prices are not discounted. They are the *normal* price. They are the price the item always costs. The fast food chain is merely trying to create an illusion of value. An illusion that by patronizing their restaurant the consumer is somehow coming out on top. I call this a dirty tactic because it is disingenuous. It’s designed to manipulate and deceive the consumer, making them believe that they are getting a good deal, when in reality, they are paying the same prices.  Another area where I believe fast food chains deploy dirty tactics is in their deceptive advertising. This is also hardly a secret. We’ve all seen the commercials. The burgers look huge and glorious, the fries are perfectly golden and piping hot, and the drinks shimmer and glisten with the promise of refreshment. In reality, well it doesn’t look like that. It’s never quite the same, is it?. You might receive a burger with a wilted lettuce leaf, one that looks like it’s been sat on by a small child. The fries are cold. The drink is 90 percent ice. This is not to say that they are completely lying to you but they are using clever photography, lighting and food styling techniques to make the food look more appealing than it actually is. This creates an expectation that the actual product often fails to live up to, leading to disappointment, disappointment, and maybe a dash of betrayal. This is not only a dirty trick but an insult to one's intelligence. Fast food chains are fully aware that their food isn’t exactly gourmet and the customer is also aware. So to try and get away with these tricks is simply… cheeky.

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? I am not entirely certain why an employee would refuse to attend company parties. Company parties are usually laid back affairs with copious amount of free alcoholic beverages and finger foods. As a boss, if an employee came to me citing “religious reasons” I would immediately take what they are saying with a grain of salt. In my experience of dealing with subordinates (and occasionally bosses, with some, shall we say, colorful results), I have found that people tend to use religion as an excuse for the behaviours of other people. It's a quick way of shutting down a discussion. I've known people who claim the sabbath is on a Tuesday or that their religion forbids the consumption of chicken (but pork is fine). I would respectfully suggest that we have a chat and try to get to the bottom of what is going on. If alcohol consumption is the issue, I would make certain that a sufficient amount of non-alcoholic beverages are available and if that doesn’t work I could suggest that they skip the parties altogether. However, if an employee had some sort of social anxiety or a personality disorder, I would be very understanding. I have nothing but empathy for people who are uncomfortable in social situations. I have been there myself and I do not want to put my employees into an uncomfortable situation. As far as I am concerned being a good boss is about compromise. The only exceptions to any of the aforementioned compromises are; a lack of job productivity (in which case the conversation usually gets less charitable), extreme rudeness to their co workers, or in cases of blatant insubordination (which I don't tolerate at all).

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? I’m not really sure if this qualifies as a pet peeve, more like a collection of irksome observations, but here goes: I utterly despise, with a passion that borders on the irrational, the cinematic trend of replacing genuine, palpable tension with cheap, manufactured jump scares. The kind where a shadowy figure suddenly lunges into frame accompanied by a cacophonous screech, meant to momentarily jolt the audience out of their seats, only to dissipate the moment after. It’s the antithesis of good storytelling. The director is essentially saying to the audience, "I have no skill in building suspense or atmosphere, so here's a loud noise to compensate." It feels lazy, disrespectful of the intelligence of the viewer. It's like the cinematic equivalent of a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat: a fleeting distraction from the actual craft of illusion. Now, I am not averse to a good scare. Hitchcock knew how to do it. Spielberg, too. They understood that true terror stems from psychological unease, from the slow burn of dread, from what the audience *doesn't* see, from the anticipation of something awful lurking on the horizon. But instead, nowadays, far too many films mistake the volume of a sound effect for the depth of a scare. Another minor one is the overuse of shaky-cam, meant to enhance realism but usually just makes me seasick and miss crucial details. And last but not least, I absolutely abhor those film trailers that give away the entire plot, including the climactic moments, rendering the actual movie-watching experience redundant. It feels like a con, like being sold a gourmet meal only to discover it's already been pre-chewed. The marketing department’s enthusiasm for these plot spoiling trailers defeats the very purpose of the movie, and it truly boggles my mind why studios still employ this strategy.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? I can’t say I have ever walked out of a movie. Not even when I saw *Battlefield Earth* (2000) at the cinema. I have been tempted however. There have been movies that I have watched in the comfort of my own home that have caused me so much annoyance that I have turned them off. The problem I have with walking out is that the cinema ticket is expensive. I would begrudgingly sit through a bad movie just to get my money’s worth. What’s the point in walking out? You would have still wasted your precious time getting to the cinema, buying overpriced snacks and drinks, sitting and enduring the trailers. You might as well sit through the whole thing. And I have to admit, sometimes the movie gets better, at least for a little bit. *Battlefield Earth* didn’t get better, of course, but the cinema experience was so weird and memorable in itself that it made the whole ordeal worth it. The theatre was half full. The audience clearly had no idea what was going on. The entire duration was filled with a combination of laughter (out of confusion, not amusement) and a sort of stunned silence. A cacophony of ‘What the fuck is this?’ was the dominant sentiment. I remember a guy sitting next to me having a conversation with his friend, not about the movie, but over who could make the loudest exasperated sigh. The whole thing was surreal. So no, I've never walked out but I can see why people would. There are plenty of movies that I can think of that have made me angry.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? One of the most glaring plot holes, often cited, exists in the classic action flick, Die Hard (1988). The terrorists, led by the suave Hans Gruber, meticulously plan their heist, taking hostages and disabling security. Their primary objective? To access the Nakatomi Corporation's vault. But here's the rub: why didn't they simply cut the power? The building's vault door uses a simple combination lock. Disable the lights, the power, the security systems, and they could have gone in and out with the loot unhindered. It would have been much simpler, and less likely to be foiled by a barefoot New York City cop. Instead, they opt for a complex scheme involving explosions, hacking, and a lot of unnecessary violence. The whole thing seems overly convoluted when a simple power outage would've sufficed. Another, more recent, offender is the critically acclaimed Christopher Nolan film, Interstellar (2014). The movie deals with the concept of time dilation near a black hole and the possibility of wormholes as a means of travelling across space. One major plot device involves the protagonist, Cooper, sending information, in the form of quantum data, through time to his daughter, Murph. By way of gravitational waves. The problem? The information is sent from a black hole *before* Cooper actually enters it. There are whole heaps of time travel paradoxes but the basic idea is that, according to the film's own internal logic, the data should never have arrived. Because the crucial event of Cooper entering the black hole and generating the necessary black hole communication was yet to occur. These are, of course, nitpicks, the stuff of armchair film critics, and they didn't stop these movies from being incredibly entertaining. But sometimes, the cracks in the narrative are just too big to ignore.

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? There are so many actors and actresses who come and go in Hollywood like shooting stars. Some fizzle out after a promising debut, others get a few good roles and then fade into obscurity, and a few struggle to consistently land impactful roles. It’s a harsh industry, and even if they are successful, the fickle whims of the audience and the studios can quickly turn against you. One name that springs to mind is Taylor Kitsch. He was supposed to be a huge deal. For some, the role of Tim Riggins in *Friday Night Lights* was his peak. While he’s still working, he never really translated that small-screen popularity to big-budget blockbusters. Kitsch had the looks, the talent, and the physique to be a leading man, but something just never clicked. His career trajectory is a classic example of a lack of momentum and the inability to find a role that truly resonated with audiences after his initial success. Then there’s Freddie Prinze Jr. He had that mid-90s, early-2000s teen heartthrob thing going on, particularly in films like *She’s All That* and the *Scooby-Doo* movies. He was a staple on teen magazine covers, dating one of the hottest actresses at the time, and his career seemed set. But Prinze Jr. never transitioned to more mature roles, and his appeal eventually faded. He didn't have the range needed to survive the shifting tides of Hollywood. Another would be Jai Courtney, touted as a rising action star. He had the physique, the chiseled jawline, and he did get some high-profile roles in things like *Suicide Squad* and *Terminator: Genisys*, but he just never quite broke through. Often his performances were wooden, and it seemed he just didn’t have the charisma to carry a film. I would say he's a talented supporting actor, but not a leading man. Finally, consider Josh Hartnett. He was everywhere at the start of the millennium, starring in a string of hits like *Pearl Harbor*, *Black Hawk Down*, and *40 Days and 40 Nights*. He certainly had the ‘it-factor.’ Though the reason for his almost complete vanishing act has never been definitely confirmed, there have been whispers over the years that he may not have enjoyed or been comfortable with the level of fame that came with his early success. He was supposed to be the next big thing. He chose to step away. It's a shame as a good actor.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? Oh, I’ve had a few stints in the fast food industry myself, back in my younger days. Let me tell you, it’s a mixed bag from behind the counter regarding those repeat customers. There are the regulars, bless their hearts, who are practically part of the furniture. You know their order by heart, you've memorized how they take their coffee, what kind of modifications they need on their burgers (hold the pickles, extra onions, no mayo, the works), and more often than not, you’ve also learned their names. Sometimes you even know what’s up with their lives, the kids, the spouse, the job, everything. They’re the ones who make the job somewhat bearable, the occasional friendly face in a sea of impatient, hangry patrons. Then there are the daily customers, the ones who seem to subsist solely on burgers and fries. You start wondering about their health, questioning their sanity, and if they have any tastebuds left. You see them day in, day out, and sometimes, you can’t help but feel a twinge of pity for them. Are these people lonely? Do they have nothing better to do? Are they trying to tell us something? As the days turn into weeks, you get to know them better. You might even strike up a conversation while waiting for those greasy burgers. They can be interesting people, but you also have to be careful since some of them are also crazy. It is truly a paradox. But they are still part of the job.

What is legal but ethically wrong? Many things. In Trinidad & Tobago, as in most places, “the law” is an imperfect construct, a series of rules and regulations that attempt to codify morality and societal expectations. However, legality and ethics often diverge, sometimes dramatically. Think of the multitude of loopholes exploited by corporations to minimize their tax obligations. Perfectly legal, yet ethically questionable, especially when such practices deprive the state of vital resources for public services like healthcare and education. Or consider the sale of certain products, like sugary drinks and processed foods, which, while legal, contribute significantly to public health crises such as obesity and diabetes. Companies are often more concerned with profit than with the well-being of their consumers. Then there are the actions of powerful individuals, like politicians who use their influence to benefit themselves or their inner circles. Perfectly within the bounds of the law, perhaps, but undeniably unethical. Nepotism, cronyism, and the blatant disregard for the public good exemplify this. Even more commonplace are situations involving intellectual property. Copyright law, in specific instances, might prevent the free use of content that could be viewed as beneficial, or even essential, for others. The laws around this can often favor corporate interests over the common good. Ultimately, the intersection of law and ethics is a complex and often murky space but a fascinating area of debate.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? There are a number of films out that could qualify for this title but my immediate answer is Alejandro Jodorowsky's *Holy Mountain* (1973). The film is a fever dream of esoteric spiritualism, religious symbolism, and surreal imagery that is utterly captivating and, to be honest, somewhat indescribable. To watch it is to enter a world where dwarfs with golden faces play the part of Christ, where frogs are used to perform rituals, and where a thief, portrayed by Jodorowsky himself, seeks enlightenment through alchemical transformation. The plot, if you can call it that, follows the thief as he is guided by a mysterious alchemist through a series of bizarre and often violent trials to reach the Holy Mountain, where he hopes to achieve immortality. *Holy Mountain* is not merely a film; it is an experience, a cinematic acid trip that leaves one questioning reality itself. It doesn’t conform to traditional narrative structure, relying instead on striking visuals, symbolism, and a relentless barrage of the unconventional. The film is almost intentionally obtuse – it's challenging, even alienating at times. But those that are willing to embrace the bizarre and surrender to Jodorowsky’s vision will find a cinematic journey unlike any other. It's a film you don’t just watch; you let it wash over you, seep into your subconscious. You grapple with its layers, its meanings, or the lack thereof, long, long after the credits roll. *Holy Mountain* is beautiful, disturbing, and profoundly thought-provoking. It’s the kind of film that stays with you, haunting your dreams with its glorious madness. It’s a reminder that cinema, at its best, can be a portal to the utterly inexplicable.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? Gollum from *The Lord of the Rings*. He is one of the most complex characters ever written, by any author. He is a twisted, pathetic creature, a shadow of his former self, consumed by the corrupting influence of the One Ring. Yet, in the moments when the ring's hold loosens, a flicker of his former self, the hobbit Smeagol, shines through, eliciting a modicum of pity. It's a testament to Tolkien's genius that he made such a damaged, vile creature so undeniably compelling. He's a cautionary tale, a reflection of the destructive power of obsession and greed, of the ways we can be utterly consumed by our desires. And the way Andy Serkis played him! Just, *chef's kiss*. Absolutely phenomenal. Despite being a villain, you actually empathise with Gollum. You see his internal struggle, his torment, his desperate clinging to the only thing that gives him any sense of meaning. He is an embodiment of so much that is wrong with human nature and that makes him more human than most of the heroes found in literature. His split personality, his internal dialogue, his constant battle between good and evil, are all so relatable. We all have a Gollum within us, you know? A shadow self, lurking in the darkness, waiting to seize control. Anyway, I believe Smeagol/Gollum is such a compelling character precisely because he is not a simple villain. He is a nuanced, troubled soul whose actions are the tragic consequence of a series of unfortunate events, bad choices and a magical ring. If he wasn't created, I'm sure this character would be one that would be sorely missed.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? The question itself is somewhat loaded. There's the assumption that Brad Pitt's looks and acting style, if you can call it that, would have been deemed suitable for the Golden Age of Cinema. Let's dissect that. Classic Hollywood, for lack of a better term, had well-defined aesthetics and acting conventions. There were the archetypes of the debonair leading man, the sultry femme fatale, the comical sidekick, the menacing villain etc. Actors and actresses, under studio contracts, were carefully molded, coiffed and groomed to fit these moulds. Their off-screen lives were strictly controlled as well. Studio heads would manufacture romances and scandals to boost ticket sales and the actor's public image. Brad Pitt, in his heyday, had a certain rough-hewn allure, a relaxed charisma that worked wonders for his career. His acting, however, was, and still is, somewhat…minimalist. He relies on a few signature moves: the knowing smirk, intense stares, the slightly mumbled dialogue, the subtle gestures. He's not a classically trained actor in the vein of an Olivier, a Hepburn, or a Tracy. While Old Hollywood also had their share of stars who were more about the image than the craft (think Errol Flynn, for example), standards of the day demanded a bit more theatricality, a dash more "acting." Pitt's understated approach might have been considered too bland, too uninspired, by the studio bosses of yesteryear. Furthermore, his career trajectory, from supporting roles to leading man, mirrors the modern Hollywood system. Classic Hollywood wouldn't have necessarily allowed that evolution. You were either a star or a character actor; there was less room for navigating between the two. Perhaps, in a different timeline, with different training and studio control, Pitt could have found his niche. But, if his current body of work is anything to go by, and comparing it to the acting styles of the legendary figures of the day, I'd wager he’d have been viewed as an attractive but ultimately replaceable face.

What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? This is going to sound like a generational cliché, but when I realized that the band "Oasis" - the soundtrack to my burgeoning teenage angst - was considered "classic rock." Man, time truly does fly. It’s even more mind-boggling when I find out that some of my students have never heard of Oasis, The Beatles, or even Led Zeppelin. They'll look at me with a blank stare, as if I’d just spoken in an ancient tongue. I recall a similar experience when my own father, may he rest in peace, brought up some of his favorite musical acts from the 50’s and 60's. I had zero clue. I thought he was speaking gibberish, or maybe pulling my leg. Then I realized that my father was not actually very old. I was merely young. Now the cycle has repeated with astounding alacrity. Another moment that underscored my advancing age was when I received a text from my bank. They were informing me that I was "eligible for a credit card."

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? This question is one that I’ve pondered over the years. There are so many things to consider. Personally, I am not burdened with children so I can only speak from an outside perspective. However, I've observed friends, family, and acquaintances experience the gamut of emotions related to parenthood – from unadulterated joy to abject despair. It is a profound responsibility, bringing a new life into the world. The commitment is unwavering, the sacrifices immense.  It also forces you to question everything. Your lifestyle comes under scrutiny, and it is never the same again. Sleep becomes a luxury, spontaneity a distant memory. The financial implications alone are staggering, particularly in this day and age. Then there's the emotional toll – the constant worry, the sleepless nights, the fear of the unknown. And yet, amidst the chaos, there's undoubtedly a unique form of fulfillment; something that I suspect gives a purpose that is difficult to match. To raise a child, to witness their growth, to nurture their dreams.  However, there will be times when the world seems a little too much to bear. Watching the news, you’d be hard-pressed to disagree. Are we bringing children into a world destined to be destroyed by war, hate, and indifference? The environmental issues. Then, there's the issue of legacy. Is it selfish to deprive the world of future generations? A philosophical paradox, to be certain. As for regret, the road not taken remains a mystery – full of both allure and trepidation. I’m not sure if I’ll ever fully know.

What's the most ruthless thing a new boss has done to show he/she is in charge? I've been in the workforce for quite a while now, and I've seen my fair share of managerial machinations. One instance, in particular, stands out, a masterclass in how to establish dominance, albeit a rather distasteful one. This was during my time at a mid-sized marketing firm, where I was a junior copywriter. Our department had a reasonably laid-back atmosphere, fostered by our previous manager, a jovial chap who believed in nurturing creativity. Then came Ms. Eleanor Vance. She was, to put it mildly, a force of nature. She strode into the office on her first day, a whirlwind of tailored power suits and a gaze that could curdle milk.

If you could choose only one font which one would it be and why? This is a purely subjective query of course. If I had to choose, I would pick Helvetica. Universally accessible? Check. Highly legible across various sizes and media? Check. Aesthetically neutral, yet possessing a clean, modern appeal? Double-check. Honestly, Helvetica is just… *chef's kiss*. It's the workhorse of fonts. It doesn't demand attention, it doesn't try too hard, it just *works*. It's like that reliable friend who's always there, dependable and never disappoints. Plus, it's been around for ages, a testament to its timeless design and enduring popularity. You simply can't go wrong with Helvetica. It's the kind of font you can use for everything from a minimalist website to a lengthy research paper. Its versatility is unmatched. Other fonts, while beautiful in their own right, often come with limitations. Maybe they're too decorative for body text, or perhaps they're poorly rendered on certain devices. Not Helvetica. It just *gets* it done, no fuss, no drama. It's the epitome of typographic efficiency and reliability. In a world overflowing with design choices and options, Helvetica is a calming constant, a reassuring presence.

What are the things no one tells you about living alone? No one tells you about the sheer volume of decision fatigue. It hits you like a ton of bricks. When you live with others, there’s a natural division of labor, a shared responsibility for the mundane, the everyday choices that structure your life. "What are we having for dinner?" "Who's doing the dishes?" "When are we going to the supermarket?" These are questions that, when living alone, you, and only you, must answer. It's not just the big stuff, like deciding on a career path or whether to buy a house; it's the relentless barrage of seemingly minor choices that chip away at your mental energy. Should I eat now or later? What shirt am I wearing today? Do I even need to wear a shirt today? It’s a constant stream of micro-decisions, and they add up. Then there’s the loneliness, a quiet, insidious thing. You might think you relish solitude, and in many ways, you do. But the silence, the empty space, the lack of a shared presence, can become a heavy burden. No one tells you how much you'll miss the random, spontaneous interactions, the shared laughter, the unexpected conversations that pepper the day when you live with others. You’ll find yourself talking to the cat, the dog, the inanimate objects in your apartment, just to break the monotony. You begin to crave those fleeting moments of connection, those small sparks of human interaction. The world feels bigger, but you become isolated in it. Beyond the logistics and the emotional hurdles, no one truly prepares you for the practicalities.

Are there parents who regret having mixed-race children? I'm not sure if there are parents who *regret* but there may be parents who find themselves unprepared for certain aspects of raising mixed-race children - parents who perhaps underestimated the complexity of the task. I can only imagine the challenges that some parents face; some of these would be familiar to all parents, others are specific to the particular circumstances of raising children of mixed heritage. Parents of mixed-race children face issues such as identity formation, the challenge of racial prejudice or discrimination (which manifests differently depending on the location - what might seem the most innocent ‘joke’ back home in the US can take on a sinister edge in certain European contexts), and cultural negotiation. My experience is that the most successful parents, in my opinion, have a deep commitment to both sides of their children's heritage. They don’t necessarily have to be entirely integrated or ‘balanced’ – and indeed, that might not even be possible – but there has to be a level of profound respect for both sides of the child’s background. Many parents, especially those of mixed cultural but not racial backgrounds, might feel prepared for this. They might both be from Britain, but one has a long family history in London, whilst the other is a recent immigrant from India. Both would likely, at least hypothetically, be familiar with the same cultural touchstones: the same TV shows, the same music, the same public figures, etc. But with mixed-race couples, the cultural negotiation is not just about understanding two different cultures, it’s about understanding their intersection, the way they interact and often, clash. It is also about the specific challenges that society will bring. Consider the couple where one parent is African-American and the other is White. They may be incredibly loving, but they inhabit different social worlds, face different societal challenges, and may even have diverging views on race relations. If the couple is from, say, the American South, they would need to actively and thoughtfully prepare their child for a world that could be more challenging than they ever expected. They might themselves be unaware of this. Often, you will hear of people's experience with racism, and it’s clear that they had no prior experience of it themselves. If the pair are from the Caribbean the challenges would be different but still very substantial. When one parent is Black and the other is Indian, the child must be equipped to handle potentially hostile attitudes from people of both racial backgrounds. The child may be met with stereotypes, prejudice, and even outright racism, not just from strangers but from family members. Perhaps, they might feel a sense of alienation from both sides of their family, as they navigate the complex world of identity and belonging. These are the crucial details, which if not carefully considered, could lead to any sort of regret.

What is an example of an album that, in your opinion, was ruined by the producer and/or the production? It's hard to pinpoint just one, as there's a graveyard of albums where the producer seemingly waged war on the artist's vision. However, the one that instantly springs to mind is Metallica's *...And Justice for All.* Now, I’m a massive Metallica fan—always have been. I can still vividly remember the first time I heard "Master of Puppets" as a teenager. That track, and the album in its entirety, consumed me, and remains one of the most important albums of all time. The follow-up *...And Justice for All,* though containing some of their most complex music, is a sonic wasteland. The bass, famously, is virtually inaudible. It’s as if the producer—fleetingly rumored to be James Hetfield, or engineer Steve Thompson—had it out for Jason Newsted. I’ve heard all the explanations over the years: "They were mad about Cliff Burton," to "Hetfield was trying to make the guitars sound heavier." Whatever, the reasons just don't hold water. This might be the only rock album I know of where the instruments that made the song powerful were an afterthought and the production was the downfall of it. The album’s best songs, “One”, “Blackened”, and “Dyers Eve”, still manage to cut through the murk, but the production actively hurts the overall experience. The drumming is so dry and sterile that it almost feels programmed, and the guitars, while up-front, lack the depth and richness that defined Metallica’s earlier work. Listening to it now, it feels like a missed opportunity, a moment where genius was squandered by carelessness or, worse, intentional sabotage of a stellar group. The album's potential was undeniable. Had the production matched the quality of the songwriting, it would have been a contender for their best work. Instead, we're left with an album that leaves you constantly fiddling with the volume knob, trying to bring the music to life. It’s a stark reminder that production is about more than just making music; it’s about sculpting sound into art.

What screams "I make terrible financial decisions!"? Buying a brand new luxury car, fully loaded, with a ten-year loan, while simultaneously being buried under a mountain of credit card debt. The car is an ostentatious display of wealth, a depreciating asset, and a constant drain on your already precarious finances, all whilst accruing interest on debt. It's the vehicular equivalent of wearing a diamond-encrusted watch while living in a cardboard box. This scenario is a symphony of poor decisions, of prioritizing appearances over solvency, of chasing the mirage of status while the foundations of financial stability crumble. The monthly payments alone would probably be enough to cover the rent of a modest apartment somewhere. The interest rate? Forget about it. It's financial self-harm, the economic equivalent of eating a diet of nothing but deep-fried desserts. The joy of owning the car will eventually fade, replaced by the relentless gnawing of financial anxiety. The realization that you've effectively mortgaged your future for temporary gratification is a bitter pill to swallow. You’re essentially paying to be miserable, to be stressed out by something that is supposed to bring pleasure. It's a vicious cycle, a downward spiral fueled by the desire to impress others, a desire that ultimately leaves you poorer, both in terms of money and peace of mind. It's a loud, screaming declaration to the world that you either lack financial literacy or have a complete disregard for the consequences of your actions.

Can you name an actor who was never a good actor but became one? Nicolas Cage. While he undoubtedly has a lengthy filmography and has even won an Academy Award, I don’t think that anyone could credibly claim that he was ever a gifted thespian. I’ve always felt that he was more of a character, an oddity, whom directors cast for his eccentricities rather than his acting prowess. But in recent times, the man, for whatever reason, has just exploded from the chrysalis of his earlier, stilted performances and has become a legitimately good actor. The films that he has done in recent years are all a testament to this unlikely transformation. I saw Pig (2021) not too long ago and it was one of the most beautifully acted films that I’ve ever seen. A performance of such quiet intensity, subtle grief. And the dude really sold the mushroom foraging. Before that was Mandy (2018). Not a good movie by any stretch of the imagination. It was more of a psychedelic assault on all the senses but Cage, at least, was brilliant in it. His over the top theatrics and his quiet stillness during the film's more introspective moments were masterfully employed. Now, the man’s career has been nothing short of interesting. He's the nephew of a certain film director. He's spent his life living off the fumes of his family name, being cast in various roles and in various genres from action blockbusters to independent dramas to thrillers to romantic comedies. In his initial acting days I was constantly left with the feeling that he was not in tune with himself, with his character and with the role at hand. It always felt like a performance rather than an expression. This man was once derided for being a bad actor and now to see his performances is like watching a phoenix reborn from the ashes. It begs the question: how can an actor suddenly unlock a new level of competence in his 50s? What was different? Perhaps he just needed the right directors, perhaps he was finally cast in roles that suited his unique persona. What I do know is that for many years it has been one of the most remarkable careers in the history of Hollywood.

What television shows started strong only to become unwatchable later? There are a few shows I can mention. But before I begin, let me state that I am often a contrarian when it comes to popular opinion. I love to have my own individual thoughts regarding media. And it is not uncommon for me to enjoy a movie or television show that is widely derided or to dislike that which is praised as a masterpiece. Let me also state that I don't mind if a show is ‘bad.’ In fact, I prefer it, sometimes. I sometimes look forward to ‘bad’ shows and have a soft spot for them, and that's what I have to say about the following show: Lost. The first season of *Lost* was must-see TV. I will concede readily. It was a phenomenon. Compelling, intelligent, mysterious, well-acted and with a cast of interesting characters. I never missed an episode, much to the chagrin of my friends and family. I was particularly smitten by Terry O'Quinn's ‘John Locke’. Season 1 to me was perfect TV. Then the writers and producers got lost, and in trying to create more mystery, became more incoherent and more bizarre, and they started making things up from episode to episode. At a certain point, I gave up caring. To finish the series, I had to endure season after season of tedium, a long, rambling, nonsensical, boring waste of time. A great premise squandered. It took a nosedive in quality. I really should have quit while I was ahead.

What's the worst experience you've had with telling someone you had feelings for them? I don't have one concrete ‘worst’ experience, but a collection of cringe-worthy moments that accumulate over time. Many of these instances occurred when I was younger, a teenager. It stemmed from a lack of self-awareness, a tendency to conflate infatuation with a grand philosophical or religious revelation. Looking back, it’s embarrassing to admit the number of times I’ve penned eloquent, angst-ridden poems or declarations of love only to be met with polite confusion or outright rejection. I recall one occasion where I attempted to express my feelings for a girl by quoting Nietzsche. Needless to say, she was more interested in the latest pop song than the intricacies of the Übermensch. On the other hand it could also be the other side of the story. I would consider myself a reasonably attractive and personable fellow. Perhaps more girls liked me more than I could ever notice. Perhaps they were too shy to say anything. One time a girl who worked as a waitress at a local coffee shop that I frequented would always give me a discount on my coffee and always smile at me when I walked in. I was oblivious. I would also sometimes ask her for song recommendations or if she had ever read any good books lately. I was that oblivious when she had no doubt a crush on me. My friends found it hilarious that I was so dense to her advances. This wasn't a ‘one-off’ occurrence. This happened to me quite a few times. As I've matured, I’ve refined my approach, opting for more direct, albeit still slightly awkward, expressions of affection. I would just ask them outright on a date and leave it at that, no long drawn out declarations of love and poetry, just a simple request and see what happens. This has led to less dramatic, yet still occasionally unsuccessful, endeavors. The key takeaway is that vulnerability, no matter how clumsily expressed, is often the starting point and you must make peace with rejection. I learned that the hard way.

Which character did you view totally differently as a child vs. as an adult? Perhaps the most potent example that readily comes to mind is the character of the Joker, particularly as portrayed by the inimitable Jack Nicholson in Tim Burton's 1989 *Batman*. As a kid, the Joker was the quintessential bad guy. He delighted in chaos, wreaked havoc upon Gotham, and, in my childish perception, was unequivocally evil, a monstrous figure who deserved to be vanquished by the caped crusader. There was no nuance, no complexity; just a black-and-white battle between good and evil, with the Joker firmly ensconced in the latter. Watching the film again as an adult, however, provided a perspective shift that was almost seismic. Now, I saw a man driven to madness, not merely for the sake of it, but by a society that had, in essence, created him. His descent into villainy felt less like a conscious choice and more like a consequence of trauma and societal neglect — in essence, the very definition of a victim. His sardonic wit, his theatrical flair, even his grotesque appearance began to take on a new dimension. I began to question the very nature of heroism and the simplistic morality of the hero/villain dichotomy. This shift in understanding was a crucial juncture in my embracing of philosophy and media analysis. I now recognized the role of the Joker as a dark mirror, reflecting back the ugliness and absurdity of the world. The laughs evoked now weren't those of unadulterated malicious glee but those of cynical recognition.

What’s your relationship with alcohol? Growing up in Trinidad, alcohol was woven into the fabric of life. From the ubiquitous rum shops on every corner to the boisterous celebrations fueled by Carib beer, it was ever-present. Alcohol wasn’t treated with the puritanical disdain I’ve witnessed in other cultures; it was simply… there. My parents were moderate drinkers, and my exposure to alcohol started early, though always in controlled, family settings. Social gatherings, be it a birthday lime or a simple Sunday cookout, were seldom without its presence. There's something intrinsically Caribbean about alcohol. It's part of a tradition, a lubricant for conversation, and a symbol of conviviality. It wasn’t, however, a means for escaping reality, as I've observed in certain settings. Drinking was about sharing, connecting, and enjoying the moment, a ritual more than a vice. As I reached adulthood, my relationship with alcohol evolved. I experienced the allure of the party scene, the reckless abandon of youth, and the occasional overindulgence that came with it. There were some nights fueled by bravado and misguided decisions, but they were few and far between. I’ve always been conscious of maintaining control.

What turns people off about Quora? I suppose there's a myriad of reasons why people might find Quora less than appealing. For starters, the signal-to-noise ratio can be atrocious. You wade through a swamp of repetitive questions, generic answers, and self-promotional drivel to occasionally unearth a gem of genuine insight. Then there's the rampant ego-stroking that permeates the platform. Some users seem less interested in sharing knowledge and more preoccupied with amassing upvotes and crafting elaborate self-aggrandizing narratives. The incessant need to be perceived as intelligent, witty, or knowledgeable can be off-putting, especially when it manifests as condescending pronouncements or thinly veiled attempts at intellectual posturing. Furthermore, the echo chamber effect is alive and well on Quora. Certain viewpoints and biases tend to dominate, leading to insular discussions and a reluctance to engage with dissenting opinions. This can create an environment that stifles intellectual curiosity and reinforces existing prejudices. I think the anonymity factor, while sometimes liberating, can also contribute to the problem. It emboldens users to make rude, inflammatory, or factually incorrect statements because they're shielded from the consequences of their actions. The lack of rigorous fact-checking and moderation doesn’t help matters either. Misinformation can spread like wildfire, and it's often left to users to debunk it, which is a losing battle at times. The platform's algorithm can be another source of frustration. It can often seem arbitrary, prioritizing sensationalism over substance and burying worthwhile content in favor of what's deemed "engaging."

Do biracial people ever pick their white side and identify as white? Speaking as a man from a Caribbean nation, with ancestry from Africa, Europe, and Asia, I can confidently say it’s a complex issue and the straight-forward answer is "yes". The question of racial identification and the “choosing” of a particular heritage, especially in the context of biracial or multiracial individuals, isn't as simple as it seems, mostly due to deeply entrenched societal perceptions. Racial identity is often shaped by a combination of factors: family upbringing, societal pressures, personal experiences, and, if you're in the diaspora, how non-biracial people perceive you determines how you choose to self-identify. For some, the choice can be largely influenced by the quest for acceptance. Let's be frank, in many societies, particularly those with a history of racial segregation or prejudice, identifying as white can provide certain privileges and advantages. It can open doors, ease interactions, and reduce, sometimes drastically, the experience of discrimination. Conversely, identifying with non-white ancestry is a form of solidarity and an acceptance of heritage. It's a balancing act, navigating the waters of identity, acceptance, and personal history. Often, the decision isn't a binary "white or non-white". Instead, it's about finding a label that best reflects one's journey and lived reality – it's about acknowledging that the concept of race is, in itself, a social construct.

What actor’s acting style has aged the worst? I'm going with the obvious pick: Nicolas Cage. He started off excellent. It wasn't only that he was blessed with his talent, he was also well-schooled. He went to the American Conservatory Theater, and he came from a family of artistic achievers. His uncle is Francis Ford Coppola, and his cousin is Sofia Coppola. He started off playing the quirky lead, the lovesick loser, the everyman with a unique neurotic bent. Think Raising Arizona (1987), Moonstruck (1987), and Honeymoon in Vegas (1992). Those were the roles that made him famous. Cage's problem is that he never adapted his acting style. He’s still playing the same roles, but everything else about him has changed. The problem is that the audience's perception of him has changed. If you've seen him in late-career productions like Willy's Wonderland (2021) and Prisoners of the Ghostland (2021), he's mostly playing himself as a cartoon character—a parody of his own style. His acting sometimes feels completely disconnected from the plot. He'll rant and rave with the most exaggerated facial expressions that don't fit the scene. He's like a jazz musician who never improvises, just plays the same riffs over and over again. His mannerisms have become his brand, but it's a brand that has grown stale. In his younger years, his eccentricity was charming, but now it feels forced and self-indulgent. He's become a meme. It's hard to watch him seriously anymore. He'll give you a wide-eyed stare, followed by a manic outburst, all while delivering lines in a bizarre, affected vocal tone. He's trapped in his own caricature. He is giving you a caricature of Nicolas Cage. Ultimately, it’s a shame. He has more than enough talent to shed the persona, but he's not doing it.

Who are the most uncomfortable movie characters depicting the UK that you’ve ever seen? I find it’s a tie. On one hand, there’s the character of Mr. Bean. He’s a walking, talking, slapstick nightmare, a social pariah disguised as a bumbling Englishman, and the embodiment of every anxiety I’ve ever felt when attempting even the most basic social interactions. His cringe-inducing antics, from turkey-on-the-head Christmas dinners to disastrous attempts at fine dining, are a masterclass in awkwardness and the utter disregard for social norms. Then again, he's quintessentially British, for better or worse. But if you want discomfort, you have to look at Del Boy from Only Fools and Horses. He and his brother are not from the aristocratic, upper class, world. Del Boy is the archetypical “nouveau riche” - a social climber, a lovable rogue perpetually attempting to elevate himself and those he loves, regardless of whether it’s through legitimate means. It’s that striving – the unyielding ambition combined with questionable ethics and constant failures that truly gets under your skin. His dodgy deals, his mangled French, his terrible car and flat, his dodgy friends; all of it is excruciatingly embarrassing to watch. The show thrives on the cringe. He's perpetually on the verge of a breakthrough, a moment of success, a flash of brilliance that always seems to elude him, and usually ends up in abject public humiliation. This is not even to mention the moments when Rodney, Del's less enterprising brother, is drawn into his schemes. Often these two character interactions involve a clash of cultures, and are often hilarious. But ultimately it's Del's relentless pursuit of something more, something better that makes him so profoundly uncomfortable to watch.

Who’s your favorite redhead? I have a soft spot for Rita Hayworth. Not just because of her crimson locks, but also because of her incredible talent. She was more than just a pretty face, though her beauty was undeniable. Her performance in *Gilda* still stands the test of time. The way she could command the screen, the subtle nuances in her expressions… just exceptional. Then there's Julianne Moore. Her versatility is astounding. She can seamlessly transition from a dramatic role to a comedic one, and always delivers a performance that feels genuine. Think about *Boogie Nights*, *The Kids Are All Right*, or *Still Alice* – each character distinct, each performance captivating. It's a testament to her skill and her ability to disappear into any role. And let’s not forget Karen Gillan. She's a contemporary favorite of mine. Her wit and charm are as fiery as her hair. From her time on *Doctor Who* to her roles in the *Guardians of the Galaxy* films and beyond, she consistently proves she's a force to be reckoned with. Plus, she's Scottish; my wife likes her accent, which is always a bonus. So, choosing a favorite is tough, but these three are the first to come to mind. Each one, a unique blend of talent, charisma, and striking red hair.

What are the cleverest scams you have come across? A particular fraud that still manages to both amuse and appall me involved a fellow I knew during my university days. He was what one would call a ‘serial entrepreneur’ – that is, a guy who was always flitting from one questionable business venture to the next. He had a magnetic personality; affable, quick-witted, and with a gift for gab that could charm the birds from the trees. His schemes, however, were less impressive, typically involving a quick profit with little regard for the law or the people he was conning. One such scheme involved a shipment of, to put it mildly, ‘slightly used’ electronics. He somehow managed to convince a group of budding tech enthusiasts that he had access to a cargo of refurbished gadgets and components from a major corporation’s liquidation. He made a killing selling this ‘high value’ tech at below market prices. The thing was, the cargo, while seemingly legitimate, including branded boxes and official-looking documents, was actually filled with cheap knockoffs and broken pieces. He had gone to great lengths to make them appear the real thing. I'm not entirely sure how he pulled it off, but he somehow sourced the appropriate packaging and even produced credible-looking invoices and shipping manifests. This involved finding a third party, most likely operating from a far eastern country, using their access to the supply chain to make convincing enough replicas but enough for a quick buck for everyone involved. The man was a master of deception. The most frightening aspect of his fraud was the sheer audacity. He would sell to the same people, time after time, and they’d be back for more. He’d move the same batch of broken electronics to them and get away with it due to his persuasive manner. They seemed to trust him implicitly, convinced by his charm and the semblance of legitimacy he so artfully constructed. It was a testament to his skill. Eventually, of course, it all came crashing down. His success meant that more unscrupulous characters became involved, each one trying to double-cross the other and take more than their share of the revenue. Word got back to the authorities, and he had to make a hasty exit from the country, leaving behind a trail of shattered trust and a legacy as colourful as it was murky. He now lives somewhere in Southeast Asia, presumably, involved in another scam, and I sometimes wonder if he ever looks back on his career and chuckles at how brazen he was.

What is the weirdest thing you've ever witnessed a parent do? My paternal grandmother was a woman of formidable will, possessed of a razor-sharp wit and a conviction in her beliefs—a quality I now understand, at my age, is often mistaken for sheer stubbornness. One day, she decided that the family was watching too much television. We did. It was the 80s. The television was the undisputed hearth of family life. This was during the glorious years of Knight Rider, MacGyver, and Miami Vice. Every child, from the age of five upward, knew which channel each show was on and the exact time it came on. Saturday morning cartoons, those precious hours of uninterrupted entertainment, were sacrosanct. My grandmother, however, declared war. She began by removing the batteries from the remote control. Not a huge deal, we thought. We could still get up and change the channel. The next step was more drastic: she hid the remote entirely. We searched high and low but to no avail. Desperate, we resorted to the ancient art of channel surfing, manually toggling through the channels on the television set itself. But my grandmother had anticipated this move. She had removed the buttons from the television. We were truly at war. We were prisoners in a home with nothing to do but talk to each other, read books, play outside and do each other’s homework. After an entire week spent without the glorious television, she called us all into the living room. She returned the buttons and the remote. She brought out a cake and a large bottle of soda. "Did you all learn your lesson?" she asked, with a sly twinkle in her eye. We eagerly nodded in unison. It was a strange victory, but a victory nonetheless. She smiled, then said, "Now let’s watch some television." And we did.

What is one thing that all men hate? Speaking from personal experience, men, in general, detest the feeling of being unequivocally wrong, particularly when the subject matter aligns with their perceived expertise or area of interest. It’s an ego-bruising experience, a direct challenge to their self-image of competence, and an unwelcome assault on their established worldview. No man, however secure or humble, relishes being publicly corrected, especially by someone they deem less knowledgeable or experienced. The ensuing discomfort is amplified tenfold if the correction involves significant, foundational concepts, something that shatters his carefully curated narrative of understanding.  Furthermore, men often harbor resentment towards unsolicited advice, especially when it concerns areas they already believe they have mastered. The implication that they need assistance or direction can be interpreted as a questioning of their capabilities, leading to defensiveness or outright rejection of suggestions. This aversion is intensified when the advice is delivered in a condescending or patronizing tone. Regardless of the advice's merit or genuine intent, the perceived disrespect overshadows its potential value. It is not about the advice; it is about the perceived erosion of their autonomy and self-sufficiency. Finally, men, at least the ones I know, possess a deep-seated aversion to inefficiency and wasted time. Any activity or situation that prolongs a process, impedes productivity, or offers minimal return on investment evokes considerable frustration. This stems from the societal pressures associated with being a ‘provider’ and a ‘doer’. Time is money, as the old adage goes, and any non-productive use of that time is seen as a threat to both individual and familial well-being. This sentiment is particularly pronounced in a society characterized by constant demands and the relentless pressures to achieve.

What was the "I'm done" moment in your last relationship? It's not easy trying to pinpoint the exact moment when the lightbulb flickers on, illuminating the end of things. Relationships, like aging wine, sour gradually. The subtle shifts in the atmosphere, the quiet resentments that bubble beneath the surface, the erosion of respect – these are the telltale signs that the finish line is in sight. But if I were to select a definitive "I'm done" moment, it would be the culmination of a pattern, a slow burn that eventually burst into flames. My ex had a penchant for cancelling plans at the last minute, always with some flimsy excuse that sounded more like a hurriedly constructed white lie. It wasn't just the cancellations, it was the lack of consideration, the disregard for my time, the implicit message that whatever came up was more important. After a series of such incidences, I asked myself, 'Am I really that unimportant?' It was a rhetorical question; I already knew the answer. I was exhausted. Being constantly disappointed, being constantly second-guessed, constantly left to pick up the pieces, after every broken date. I didn't owe her my time or patience. It's tough enough dealing with the world, but to discover your own partner doesn't have consideration for you is a cold slap to the face. The final straw, the moment that hammered home the reality of it all came when she cancelled a preplanned birthday dinner I'd arranged for her over a month in advance. Something came up, apparently. I could feel my heart sink. Then again, as it was sinking, it was also soaring. Freedom felt glorious. I ended it there and then. With all the grace and poise of a man ordering a double shot of whisky, with an ice cube, neat.

What makes you cringe internally? The other day I was at a local family restaurant. It was the kind of place where the service was slow and the food was middling at best, but the atmosphere was comforting and familiar like one of those timeless greasy spoons you could walk into half asleep and still know where to sit. I was there with my wife, her mother and her sister, and we were all engaged in a lively conversation. My wife had just started talking about an irritating colleague at her office when a family, seated nearby, caught my attention. The father had a habit of loudly correcting his children, the mother seemed more interested in her phone than her family, and their two kids were running amok. The older one, a girl of about seven, was loudly arguing with the parents while the boy, perhaps five or six, had started to cry. And here’s where the cringe started for me. The father, in the most condescending voice, started to tell them both to stop being dramatic, they were being ridiculous and that other people were watching. He kept repeating, "Stop it. Stop It." in a voice that oozed exasperation. The mother kept at her phone without even looking up. The girl, seeing that she was going nowhere, started to eat. The boy, red faced and sniffling, sat and stared at an empty point in the corner of the restaurant, the tears now frozen on his face. The father, seeing that the situation was defusing, looked at us with exaggerated exaggerated look of, ‘Can you believe these kids?’ He gave the impression that his children were the rudest children that ever existed and that he was an unfairly burdened saint for being in their presence. I couldn’t understand why anyone saw themselves in such a way. Then, the little girl, perhaps catching on to what her parents were doing, went to the condiments section and started pouring ketchup on her head and smearing the stuff on her face. It was a silent act of rebellion. The parents did not notice it or if they did, they chose to ignore it. At that very moment, I decided to find a quiet, private internal cringe. I got out my phone, ignored my family and went on Quora.

What was a red flag that made you stop talking to a person immediately? There was this girl I was seeing for a few weeks. She was bright, attractive, funny, and we shared many common interests. She’d regale me with tales of her globetrotting adventures through Europe and South America. She spoke multiple languages, and I was impressed. It’s not often you meet someone with genuine cosmopolitan experience. One evening we were having dinner at a rather upscale restaurant. We were having a jovial conversation when she suddenly stopped, stared at her plate, and sighed dramatically. “This lobster,” she said, “is just so… *blah*.” I was taken aback. I’d never heard a food described with such vacuousness. I asked her what she meant by that. She couldn’t articulate what she was looking for. She just went on a tangent about how she was such a foodie and how she had been “*spoiled*” with the best cuisines around the world. Fine, I thought to myself. To each his or her own, but the way the comment was delivered and the tone in which it was offered annoyed me. But, I brushed it aside thinking that maybe she was just having a bad day. We were walking back to the car and she pointed at a homeless person begging for money. She made a face that was probably meant to imply sympathy, but it came off as disgust. “Ugh,” she said, “it’s people like *that* that make me ashamed to be a human being.” I was stunned into silence for about three or four seconds. This was a red flag for me. This was the type of moment that made me realize I had better things to do with my time. I ended the relationship not long after. There was a clear lack of empathy and an inability to see the world through someone else's eyes. I wasn’t looking for a saint, but I certainly wasn’t looking for someone who would openly disparage others.

What is the strangest thing a truck driver has seen while driving? The strangest thing I've ever heard a truck driver saw happened to a guy I knew in my university’s Agribusiness Management program. He was from a small town in the south of Trinidad. One of the few in our class from the countryside, he was as laid-back as they come. He was your stereotypical Trinbagonian fella - easy going, jovial and had a penchant for partying. But on this specific occasion he was working as a long-haul truck driver. He said that one night he was driving the Beetham Highway, heading east, towards the highway leading to the airport. This was in the early morning hours, approximately 2:00 am - 3:00 am. Now, on any ordinary day, the Beetham Highway is already a bizarre place. It's a very heavily industrialized area, and it's also the location of a major squatter settlement. Because of the numerous car repair workshops, auto parts stores, tyre shops etc a constant flow of light traffic is taking place even at that time of night. So, despite the squalor, it's generally considered a safe place to drive. My friend was driving along, minding his own business. He then notices a man dancing in the middle of the road. Not just any kind of dancing, but a most elaborate performance, complete with pirouettes and ballet leaps. The man was wearing some sort of white cloak or gown. He was not concerned about the oncoming vehicles, as he elegantly danced, oblivious to the potential danger. My friend swore he saw a sort of aura emanating from the man, but he couldn't be certain. He was quite perplexed. He stopped his truck. The dancing man, without breaking rhythm, made his way towards the truck and started knocking on the window. The dance was now less elegant and bordering on frenetic. My friend, thinking he was about to be mugged, hastily locked the doors. The man continued to knock, gesturing that he needed to come in. My friend, frozen with fear, refused to budge. Eventually the man gave up and, spinning around, disappeared into the darkness. No one knows what that was. Nobody has ever reported seeing a cloaked ballet dancer on the Beetham Highway. My friend has no reliable explanation for this, but the man was never seen again.

Did you ever stop caring about how old you are? As a child, I had an obsession with birthdays. It was a source of great pride to me to be a year older than all my friends. I’d constantly ask my parents for my birthday, the precise year, month, date, and time that I was born. As I grew older, that fascination waned, like many ephemeral childhood passions. Now, I’m indifferent. I no longer keep track of my age, even my own; I usually have to do some mental calculations when prompted. I still enjoy my birthday, and I appreciate any well wishes I receive. The older I get, the more I find that celebrating a birthday, or any other special occasion, is an excellent excuse to simply relax and appreciate the good things in life, but, ultimately, the specifics of the date are irrelevant. The relentless march of time, though, affects everyone, and one becomes more aware of its impact on the body and mind. I may not care about the year on the calendar, but I’m always cognisant of the passage of time.

What is your scariest driving on a dark and lonely road at night story? One night, while driving home from my university campus after a late library session, I was traversing a particularly desolate stretch of highway. The road was enveloped in an inky blackness, punctuated only by the feeble glow of my headlights and the distant, eerie flicker of isolated streetlamps. The sky was overcast, adding to the oppressive atmosphere of the evening. It was the kind of night where the silence felt almost tangible, broken only by the rhythmic hum of my car’s engine and the occasional rustle of unseen creatures in the surrounding bush. I was lost in thought, replaying the day’s lectures in my mind, when I noticed something out of the corner of my eye. A figure, or what appeared to be a figure, standing on the side of the road, partially obscured by shadows. My first thought was, "Oh, great, a stranded motorist. Why always me?"

What are the best episodes of the original Twilight Zone TV series? The original *Twilight Zone* series remains, in my estimation, one of the greatest television shows ever made. I am of the opinion that its best episodes are not the ones that are inherently 'scary' but the ones that are the most thought-provoking. The show's genius stemmed from its ability to use science fiction, horror and fantasy to address serious social issues of the day. It was a show that possessed a profound understanding of the human condition and presented it in the most compelling way. It has a wealth of episodes to choose from, but I'll narrow down my favourites. Firstly, *The Monsters are Due on Maple Street.* It's an indictment of paranoia, mass hysteria and the dangers of conformity. The inhabitants of a suburban street turn on each other when the power goes out, believing aliens have infiltrated their community. Some of the most harrowing moments of the series came not from monsters, but from ordinary people at their worst. This episode, with its chilling conclusion, remains remarkably relevant decades later. *Eye of the Beholder* is unforgettable. It presents a world where the definition of beauty is twisted, and the protagonist's disfigurement (by the standards of that world) leads to a moving reflection on societal standards. This episode features a remarkable twist ending and a stunning performance from Donna Douglas. *The Hitch-Hiker* is a masterclass in suspense. A young woman driving cross-country is pursued by a mysterious hitch-hiker who seems to appear at every turn. The episode's tension is palpable, and its exploration of mortality and the fear of the unknown remains deeply unsettling. *To Serve Man* is deservedly famous, with its memorable reveal that, despite what we thought, the aliens never truly came in peace. Although it is somewhat of a cliché to include it on lists like these, some episodes are timeless for a reason and this is definitely one of them. As a final mention, *Living Doll* is a bone-chilling story featuring a domineering stepmother and a malevolent talking doll. It plays into a fear of the seemingly innocent and the notion that the most dangerous people are often the ones who appear harmless. There are so many other brilliant episodes that narrowly missed out on this list, but as I said, I needed to narrow it down. It's almost a shame that this list is finite because I could go on for days.

Was Shelley Duvall considered attractive? Shelley Duvall, a name synonymous with quirky cinematic brilliance, remains a fascinating figure, and the topic of her perceived attractiveness certainly sparks debate. Beauty, after all, resides firmly in the eye of the beholder, doesn't it? The question is interesting precisely because her on-screen persona, particularly in films like *3 Women* or *The Shining*, often showcased an ethereal, sometimes unsettling, almost otherworldly beauty rather than a conventional one. Hollywood, notoriously fickle, frequently casts actors based on a narrow spectrum of what it deems attractive, leading to a homogenization of appearances. Yet, Duvall, with her distinctive features - her wide, expressive eyes, her high cheekbones, and her impish grin - carved out a unique niche. She was not a conventional leading lady, but she possessed undeniable charisma, a quality that resonated with many viewers and secured her collaborations with influential directors like Robert Altman and Stanley Kubrick. One could argue that her appeal transcended physical attributes alone and that her talent and screen presence were integral to her attractiveness. She projected an undeniable vulnerability while also portraying a strength of character. She had the rare ability to be both captivating and unsettling on screen. So, the answer, as with most discussions about beauty, becomes complex. Was she conventionally attractive? Perhaps not, though many would disagree. Was she captivating? Without a doubt.

What one thing did your father do that left your mother sobbing? My parents, they weren't saints, but they were certainly characters. My father, he had a penchant for extravagant gestures, which, more often than not, backfired spectacularly. He wasn't a malicious man, just a bit… clumsy in his affections. They'd been married for what felt like an eternity, and their relationship was a tangled web of love, frustration, and stubbornness. There was this one anniversary, let's peg it around their 25th. He'd decided to be romantic, bless his heart, and planned a surprise. Now, my father, being a man of modest means and even more modest planning skills, decided to recreate the Taj Mahal in our backyard. Or at least a miniature version of it. He'd been at it for weeks, using construction scraps from his job and anything else he could scrounge.
