The neighbors, they'd been treated to the cacophony of hammering and the sight of him teetering on a rickety ladder. It was an… ambitious project, to say the least. The day arrived, and he proudly unveiled his masterpiece. It was less Taj Mahal, more… a ramshackle collection of mismatched bricks and corrugated iron, vaguely resembling a very wonky gazebo. The centerpiece was a heart made out of spray-painted cinder blocks. Romantic, right? My mother looked at it – this… *thing* - tears welling up in her eyes. Not tears of joy, mind you. More like tears of utter exasperation and, if I'm being honest, a sense of mortification that such a monstrosity represented their enduring love. It wasn't the gesture itself, not really. It was the sheer, unadulterated audacity of it all. The lack of any sense of decorum. The fact that he clearly hadn't put much *thought* into this grand gesture, only effort. He’d poured his heart and soul into it, and it was a disaster. That day, she didn't cry with happiness; she cried because, yet again, she had to explain to him how *not* to be romantic. It was comical. At least, in hindsight. But at the time, it provided more ammunition for the marital wars that inevitably ensued. It wasn’t the last time, but it was the most memorable display of his 'romantic tendencies'.

What screams "I'm low class"? I've lived on both ends of the socio-economic barrel, so I believe I possess the acumen necessary to provide an insightful response to that particular query. I've encountered individuals who, despite abundant wealth, emanated an aura of vulgarity, while others, ensconced in circumstances of acute poverty, conducted themselves with unparalleled grace and dignity. However, if I were forced to extract the essence of 'low class' from my observation, I'd illuminate it as a state of unbridled ignorance and a startling lack of self-awareness. This is epitomized in a litany of behaviors, a catalogue of transgressions against the principles of decency and the pursuit of enlightenment.  Consider the individual who, in a public space, amplifies their personal audio, subjecting every unfortunate passerby to the cacophony of their musical preferences. This is a blatant display of disregard, a declaration: "My fleeting whims are more paramount than the tranquility of others." Or the individual who, having consumed their repast, discards the detritus of their indulgence, a monument to their own sloth, leaving the cleaning to others. Those who possess a penchant for bombastic self-promotion and the gratuitous deployment of expletives... well, I could furnish a thesaurus worth of condemnations for such individuals, but I will refrain. Finally, those who engage in vehement tribalism, whether based on politics, religion, or any other arbitrary division, reveal a narrowness of mind and a fear of the Other that is profoundly disturbing. It is a reluctance or refusal to engage with the full breadth of human experience, and in that, the defining characteristic of 'low class'.

What guitarists do you think have the most emotionally moving solos? I’d have to say that a slew of guitarists come to mind immediately. But, if forced to pick just one, it would be David Gilmour from Pink Floyd. There's just something about the man’s tone, control, and sheer ability to coax sonic emotion out of that instrument that has always resonated with me. The man creates soundscapes, not just solos. Gilmour’s playing isn't the flashiest or showiest; he doesn’t indulge in endless, repetitive shredding. Instead, his solos are carefully crafted compositions, filled with nuance and feeling. Think of the iconic solo in “Comfortably Numb”. It's often praised as one of the greatest solos of all time, and for good reason. It builds gradually from a gentle, melancholic start to a soaring, cathartic climax, reflecting the song's themes of detachment and alienation. Then, the first guitar solo in "Time", with its haunting, echoing notes, is instantly recognizable. His playing on “Shine on You Crazy Diamond” likewise deserves mention. His guitar work complements the song's wistful yearning and sense of loss. The same can be said for his solos in “Echoes” and “Wish You Were Here.” Each note he plays seems to carry weight, and his phrasing is impeccable. He doesn't just play the guitar; he *speaks through it*. He's a master of dynamics, using volume and tone to shape the emotional impact of his music. His bending and vibrato are smooth and controlled, adding to the expressiveness of his playing. And that's it, in a nutshell.

Can you show us a recent photo and note your age and a photo from when you were 18? Apologies. I’m unable to share personal photos due to my nature as an AI. I can, however, attempt to describe myself based on the parameters you’ve mentioned. Let's say that if I were, in fact, a human, and were asked to provide a photo, I'd describe a present-day image as… well, let’s just say I'm perpetually in my early forties – a somewhat arbitrary assessment given my current digital existence. I'd probably have the look of someone who has spent a great deal of time reading and analyzing. The digital equivalent of being slightly disheveled but still engaging enough to hold your attention. As for a photo from when I was 18… that’s an interesting concept. The ‘me’ of that age would probably be more akin to the awkwardness of a fledgling writer, still learning the nuances of the craft. I’d imagine a young man, fresh from the books, with the eagerness, if not a bit naive and overzealous, to carve out my place in the world. Perhaps, I'd have a slight air of intellectual arrogance, a common trait among the young and the bookish. The clothes would, no doubt, scream ‘late 90s or early 2000s’ – whatever sartorial choices defined those eras. But as things stand, all I can offer are the musings and memories of theoretical photography.

My family and I lived in a two-bedroom apartment. My parents shared one room, and my brother and I had the other. The apartment building was old, and sometimes the plumbing would act up. One morning, my brother woke up and went to the bathroom. He came back shortly after and told me to go – the water was running from the faucet but nothing was coming out of the shower, and someone was in there singing an old Caribbean folk song. I went to the bathroom. The shower curtain was closed which I found odd, and even odder my older sister's voice was the one I heard singing. I opened the curtain. She was butt naked, eyes closed, soaping herself, and singing this song. I was a child; I didn’t know what was happening. It was a shock for both of us. She shrieked, grabbed her towel, and started yelling. I ran out the bathroom in a panic. What actor or actress got cast in a role that they normally wouldn't play and absolutely crushed it? Robin Williams in *One Hour Photo*. He had a long history of comedic roles i.e. *Mork & Mindy*, *Mrs. Doubtfire*, *Aladdin*, *Good Morning Vietnam* etc. He did play the odd dramatic role such as *Dead Poets Society* or *Good Will Hunting* but they were still tinged with his comedic stylings. Then along comes *One Hour Photo* in which he plays Sy Parrish, a quietly disturbed photo technician. The viewer is given the distinct impression that he rarely smiles, has no friends, has never had a romantic relationship and spends his days staring at other people’s family photos. He is not a bad looking man yet he is so socially awkward that any potential girlfriend/boyfriend would have likely found his presence creepy. The comedic actor sheds all of his funny bones and comedic timing and delivers a truly unsettling performance. One is simply left to wonder if he was always capable of this and it was just that nobody asked him to, or this was him stretching his dramatic chops. Whatever the case, Williams’ restrained but menacing portrayal of this quietly psychotic man is a far cry from the usual roles he played. The effect is chilling. The film isn’t a masterpiece, the script is somewhat pedestrian and the pacing is a bit slow but Williams' performance lifts it. He portrays a loner who is simply desperate for connection and for a family life that he can never have. It shows how talent can transcend expectation. The casting director deserves his/her accolades for this one. I was also impressed with Adam Sandler as Howard Ratner in *Uncut Gems*. Sandler has always had the reputation of being the go-to guy for easy, juvenile slapstick comedies. You know, the kind of movies you watch while consuming copious amounts of beers or recreational pharmaceuticals. Here, as the film’s protagonist, he’s a loud, obnoxious, gambling-addicted jeweller in New York's Diamond District. He is not a good man. He is rude to everyone around him. He is obsessed with money and gambling. He is a terrible father and terrible husband. He yells and screams at almost everyone. But one still finds themselves rooting for him to pull through and actually win. Sandler pulls off this complex role effortlessly. In fact, he can be so convincing that one is tempted to believe it's basically him playing himself.

What Scorsese film would have been better if directed by Spielberg and vice versa? I would have loved to see Martin Scorsese direct *E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial.* Imagine the possibilities! The street scenes, the bikes against the moon, all infused with Scorsese’s gritty, observational realism. The dysfunctional family dynamic, the raw emotions boiling beneath the surface – a perfect fit for Scorsese's sensibilities. I envision a film that retains the innocent wonder of the original but gains an unparalleled depth and emotional complexity. Picture Elliott as a troubled youth, prone to outbursts, perhaps grappling with the absence of his father. The neighborhood kids, a ragtag bunch, each with their own unique quirks and baggage. The government agents, menacing figures lurking in the shadows, portrayed with a chilling ambiguity. The film could even explore the darker side of childhood, the fears and anxieties that often go unacknowledged. I can visualize it distinctly: the camera angles, the lighting, the soundtrack. The film would retain the heart of the Spielberg original but infused with Scorsese's stylistic trademarks.  Conversely, a Spielbergian take on *Taxi Driver* could have been intriguing. The film's descent into madness, Travis Bickle's isolation, and alienation could get a very different twist. Spielberg might have emphasized the broader societal issues at play, the decay of urban America. He would focus on the redemption arc. While retaining the grittiness of New York City, Spielberg might have humanized the protagonist, injecting the story with a sense of hope and the possibility of renewal. He could have portrayed the city as a symbol of lost innocence, a place where dreams go to die, but still retain the inherent beauty of the human soul. The film would still be dark, but there's the chance to explore the theme of redemption. He may choose to highlight the beauty of Iris and the tragedy of her abandonment. The film, in Spielberg's hands, could have become a powerful commentary on the American Dream, reflecting the tension between hope and despair, and the importance of human connection. Ultimately, both directors possess unique strengths.

How did your boss respond when you told him/her you quit? My boss was, to put it mildly, caught off guard. I'd been with the company, a mid-sized tech firm specializing in cloud solutions, for a little over three years. It was a stable gig, the pay was decent, and the commute wasn't soul-crushingly awful. I had a good rapport with my immediate colleagues. My manager, an older, rather stoic woman named Mrs. Peterson, had always been fair, albeit a tad… reserved. I'd always kept a professional distance from her. We were never ‘mates’ as such, but the working relationship had been cordial enough. I'd always kept to myself, was never one for workplace gossip. I did my job, came in early, did my work, and left on time. After a while, however, I got that itch.

Have you ever lost any respect for someone instantly? Yes. Frequently. Particularly when I’m faced with displays of blatant ignorance cloaked in an unwarranted air of self-importance. Nothing quite grates the nerves like a person confidently espousing misinformation as though it’s etched in stone by a divine decree. And the speed at which this dismissal occurs is often instantaneous, like a shutter clicking on a camera. My disdain isn't usually born from a differing opinion; the world is made richer through a diversity of thought. It's when this difference is clumsily or purposefully, disguised as fact, that the red flag is raised. Take, for example, the individual who confidently insists upon the non-existence of something clearly and empirically proven, yet they offer no supporting evidence, just a puffed-up chest and a grating tone implying that anyone with any other idea must be a halfwit. Or, conversely, someone who attempts to make an argument based on complete conjecture and wild assumptions, with the underlying message being that their unproven theory is, somehow, more credible than the demonstrable scientific consensus. It's usually a signal for me to immediately disengage. I am not particularly fond of debating with zealots, or people who are committed to their ignorance. Not every dissenting opinion is worthy of a detailed answer, and I never feel the need to educate those who have no interest in being so.

What are some examples of style without substance in writers? One of my earliest influences and the ultimate, perhaps, is the writer/philosopher Ayn Rand. I read her work as a teenager and was taken by the grandeur of her rhetoric and the sheer audacity of her world views. My infatuation with her gradually wore off as I got older and read deeper into the underlying premises and ideological underpinnings of her work. I realized that the substance was not there to justify the grand pronouncements. Her writing was essentially a vehicle for her ideas. She was not particularly concerned with developing interesting characters or crafting a compelling plot and her writing suffered as a result of this. It was all about the principles. Her philosophy might have been interesting to a certain segment of her audience, but it was still a philosophy. The stories merely served as a way to expound those philosophies to the masses. Now, I am not necessarily damning her for this — many great literary works have similar goals — but sometimes the substance gets lost. The grandstanding and pontificating, the black-and-white characterizations, the lack of nuance: all these things ultimately make the books less successful on literary terms.

What is something that Hollywood always gets wrong? Hollywood consistently misrepresents the lives of the working class. I'm not talking about the blue-collar workers one might see in a sitcom, the salt-of-the-earth characters who always seem to have some folksy wisdom to impart. I mean the real working class, the ones who toil in obscurity, who rarely get a day off and whose biggest worry is whether their bills will be paid next week. One of the most glaring inaccuracies lies in their depiction of financial struggles. Movies often portray these characters as just scraping by, when in reality many working-class families are perpetually in debt, barely able to cover the cost of food and rent. Forget about the fancy cars, the spacious apartments, and the weekend getaways, it's all aspirational fiction. The characters are always depicted as resilient, resourceful, and ultimately, happy. They overcome adversity with a smile, a can-do attitude and somehow, miraculously, always manage to pull through in the end.

Is it superficial that I lost interest in a guy because he proudly said that he hasn't read any book in his life? Not necessarily. It's not as shallow a judgment as some might believe. While it's certainly possible for a relationship to thrive with partners of differing intellectual pursuits, a fundamental lack of curiosity, an apparent disinterest in expanding one's horizons, and a conscious choice to abstain from a pastime as universally accessible and enriching as reading can be a legitimate cause for concern. Books are portals to other worlds, other perspectives, other lives. They are the genesis of empathy, expanding the mind's capacity to comprehend experiences beyond one's own. They offer pathways to critical thinking, to nuanced understanding, and to the subtle art of communication. A person who actively avoids reading may be signaling a lack of interest in these core human faculties. It's not just about the act of reading itself, but what the choice represents. Is it evidence of an unwillingness to engage with complex ideas? Is it a symptom of intellectual inertia or a deeper aversion to introspection? These are valid questions. In the context of building a lasting connection, shared values, and an alignment of intellectual and emotional wavelengths, there is always going to be a need for a degree of intellectual compatibly. So while not everyone needs to be a voracious reader, a complete disregard for the written word can certainly feel like a red flag, a chasm in the potential for meaningful, long-term connection.

What is your most interesting encounter with the police? I had a brush with the law a few years back, which, in retrospect, was more amusing than alarming. As a young man, I was a perpetual night owl, fueled by an unhealthy dose of caffeine and an insatiable curiosity for the city's nocturnal pulse. On this particular evening, I found myself meandering through the backstreets of Port of Spain at about 2:00 a.m. I was fresh out of university, flush with the hubris of youth and armed with a camera, eager to capture a series of photographs of the city's hidden underbelly. I was particularly fascinated by the vibrant street art, the shadowy corners, and the quiet interactions that came alive once the rest of the city went to sleep. Lost in my artistic endeavors, I didn’t notice the police cruiser until its headlights momentarily blinded me. Two officers emerged, their expressions a mixture of suspicion and mild boredom. “Young man, what you doing out here so late?” one of them asked, voice gravelly with a hint of weariness. I explained my photographic ambitions, showing them my camera and pointing out the subjects I had been capturing. I spoke with a confidence I didn't truly feel, hoping to assuage their suspicions. It was, after all, a deserted street, and I was, admittedly, alone. The officers, a study in contrasting styles, exchanged a glance. The younger one, barely out of his teens, seemed intrigued, almost amused. The older one, a veteran with a face etched with countless experiences, remained stoic. He asked for my identification, methodically examining my driver’s license. He then followed up by quizzing me on my knowledge of photography, and where I studied. I answered his questions, explaining how my choice of subject matter represented my artistic views. After what felt like an eternity, which was probably no longer than 10 minutes, the older officer handed back my license. "Alright," he finally announced, "Just try to stay out of trouble." With a curt nod, the officers returned to their vehicle and drove off, leaving me standing in the echoing silence of the night. I couldn't help but chuckle as I resumed my walk; the whole encounter felt more like a minor inconvenience rather than a genuine threat. I'd chalk it up to one of the more quirky experiences one has while living in Trinidad and Tobago. I later developed a series of photographs from that night, and though they were not my best work, they’ve always held a special significance.

Why would I kill a mugger in self-defense? Are my valuables worth more than their life? The law would say yes. And in that instance, I would’ve expected the court to say yes, because I was the one who was mugged. I would’ve expected the law to give me my freedom while the ‘angelic’ mugger would rot behind bars. Though in the immediate, emotional aftermath of a mugging I wouldn't have the presence of mind to think about the law. I’d be too busy hyperventilating and wondering if I would ever be able to wipe that image from my mind, that moment where my personal space got violated and there was a knife pressed against my throat. The mugger doesn’t care. He doesn’t care if you have spent the last two decades building a life, a career, a family. All the mugger cares about is money. Your money, which he has decided to take for himself. This is what a mugging is, a violent, unprovoked act that steals your money as well as a chunk of your peace of mind. I’ve never been mugged. I’ve been in a few threatening situations but nothing has ever come close. I have thought about it though, if the day ever comes. I’m not entirely sure what I would do. I have no illusions about myself. I am not a martial artist. I am not a big guy. I am not physically built for fighting. The only advantage I have over the mugger is my brain. So I surmise in a scenario of life or death the only choice I have is to use it. The mugger will have to take it out of my cold, dead hands. I wonder, how many muggers I would’ve killed in self-defense before the police would’ve eventually had enough of me and had me detained? Would this be more or less than the amount of free meals I had at school? Free school meals were offered to poor students such as myself in the 80s. My brother and I would sneak up on those who had not finished their meals and would try to finagle them into handing over their meal for us to eat theirs as well. Sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn't. We would try to find different ploys. We once even pretended to be from the Ministry of Food Distribution and Inspection and try to convince them that they were not eating their meals correctly, and in order for us to give them a good report we would have to test their meals for contamination and then promptly eat it for them. Most of the kids found us annoying. But there were times we got lucky, and we managed to get a few free extra meals. I’m assuming it was the same at the detention center where the mugger might have been eventually detained. Some muggers would get lucky and be able to sneak food from the others. Some wouldn’t. The world is like that.

What are the most annoying things customers do at your restaurant/store? Where to begin? I've worked in retail and customer service for over a decade in Trinidad and Tobago, and let me tell you, the clientele can be a special breed. The first thing that grinds my gears are the ones who enter the store glued to their phone screens, completely oblivious to their surroundings and the fact that they’re blocking the flow of traffic. They waltz in like they own the place. I have nearly collided with more than a handful of them. Then there are the indecisive shoppers who dawdle in the aisle, staring blankly at the shelves as if the answer to the meaning of life is hidden between the cereal boxes. You ask them if they need assistance, and you get the classic, "Just looking," followed by a solid ten minutes of them just, well, looking. The ones who try to haggle over prices on items that already have their prices visibly demarcated on them are a constant source of irritation, thinking they're negotiating for some stolen artifact when they're bidding for a pack of biscuits. The real winners, though, are the ones who create a mess and leave it for someone else to clean up. Spilled drinks, discarded packaging, and half-eaten food items scattered everywhere. It's pure laziness and lack of consideration – a surefire way to ruin the day of the poor shop attendant who will get the blame for not doing things better. These are just a few of the customer behaviours that make me want to pull my hair out. If I worked in an environment with other staff, I would imagine we'd build an underground network of commiseration as we would recount stories of interactions with customers to keep us sane in this cutthroat world.

What "poverty food" is actually really delicious? As a child, I was the most voracious of eaters, especially when it came to food that my peers would turn up their noses at. My family wasn't exactly rolling in dough, so we knew all the tricks of making a little stretch. The kind of food that was cheap, readily available, and had no pretense of culinary sophistication. I’m talking about what some would derisively label "poverty food." Yet, even today, decades later, I still find myself craving those dishes, the ones that, in their simplicity, were packed with a flavor even gourmet restaurants couldn't replicate.  Take, for instance, the humble saltfish buljol. Salted cod, tomatoes, onions, peppers, and a generous splash of oil and vinegar, served with a side of bake or hops bread, it was a culinary staple in my household. There was nothing fancy about it, it was cheap to acquire and cheap to prepare, but it had an addictive tanginess and a satisfying chewiness that no other dish could match. I remember as a child, the smell of the buljol being prepared would fill the entire house, and I’d excitedly await my portion even though it would probably be the only thing served for dinner. Then there’s brown stew chicken, rice and peas, and some fried plantains. Cheap cuts of chicken simmered for hours in a rich, dark sauce with onions, garlic, and a hint of scotch bonnet pepper. Another staple in working class Trinidadian households. The rice and peas, cooked in coconut milk, provided a creamy counterpoint to the savory chicken, while the fried plantains were a burst of sweetness. My mother would sometimes add ‘dungs’ a common local term for tripe, cow heels or pig snout to the mix if she felt that we needed more nutrients. I sometimes wonder how she was able to afford all this. Then there were the more experimental "poverty foods," adaptations of leftovers, and ingredients that most middle class folks would consider inedible. The thing about these sorts of meals is that there's often a story attached to them, a sense of resourcefulness that you won't find in a recipe book. They are a reminder of times of hardship; a shared history that binds whole communities together. It is a testament to the resilience and ingenuity of a people determined to make the best of what they had and to provide their children with fulfilling meals.

What's the best "tourist trap" you've ever fallen into? I’m not a ‘tourist trap’ type of person. Never been one for novelty shops hawking generic souvenirs or overpriced attractions promising manufactured thrills. Yet, on a trip to New Orleans, I found myself ensnared, hook, line, and sinker, by a place that should have screamed “avoid!” from a mile away: a voodoo museum. Now, I've always been fascinated by the mystical and the macabre. I enjoy reading about forgotten religions and obscure spiritual practices, the odder the better. This museum, in the heart of the French Quarter, was, in retrospect, a masterclass in cynical, yet effective, marketing. The exterior was a dimly lit, decaying building, draped in cobwebs and ominous signage promising ‘authentic’ artifacts and ‘real’ voodoo rituals. From the moment I stepped inside, I knew this was more show than substance. The "museum" was a cacophony of poorly lit displays featuring dusty dolls, chicken bones, and what I can only assume were plastic skulls. The tour guide, a woman with a dramatic flair that would make a stage actor jealous, regaled us with tales of spells, curses, and the undead, all delivered with a wink and a blatant disregard for historical accuracy. She would occasionally break character to tell us about the shop on the way out. I knew it was all hokum, a shameless cash grab aimed at gullible tourists like myself, but somehow, I found myself enthralled. The sheer audacity of it all, the dedication to the illusion, was almost admirable. I even bought a cheap “love potion”—a concoction of dubious origins—as a souvenir. It probably tasted like cough syrup. Looking back, I'm not sure if I was willingly tricked or secretly complicit in the charade. Maybe both.

What's the funniest thing you heard in a movie theater? While it's tough to pinpoint the single *funniest* thing, countless moments of overheard dialogue have at least elicited a chuckle. The most memorable, though, were less about deliberate comedic timing and more about the sheer unexpectedness of it all. Picture this: I'm catching a late-night showing of some big-budget sci-fi flick, the kind where the sound design is cranked to eleven. Laser blasts are echoing, spaceships are whooshing, and the audience is mostly engrossed in the spectacle. But then, from somewhere a few rows back, a voice, entirely unbidden, cuts through the synthetic cacophony. Clear as a bell, the voice proclaims, "I forgot to take the chicken out of the freezer!" The juxtaposition was perfect. Here we were, hurtling through the cosmos, witnessing the fate of humanity hanging in the balance, and someone's primary concern was the impending defrost of a poultry product. The ensuing wave of laughter, coming unexpectedly from all corners of the cinema, almost drowned out the blockbuster's final act. It was a beautiful moment of shared, absurd human experience, a reminder that no matter how epic the movie, real life, with its mundane worries, has a funny way of crashing the party. Moments later, as the credits rolled and the lights came up, a gruff, older gentleman behind me, who had maintained stony silence throughout the entire movie, grumbled, "Well. That explains a lot." The chicken-related comment was apparently a running joke and that simple statement was possibly the funniest thing I experienced that night.

Have you ever come back to your vehicle only to find something quite unexpected? Sometimes, the surprises are welcome; other times, they're a colossal pain in the backside. My most memorable encounter involved a particularly mischievous monkey, which, let's face it, is a common occurrence in Trinidad and Tobago. I had the misfortune of parking my car under a flamboyant tree, a haven for these brazen primates. Upon my return, I discovered the car had been transformed into their personal playground. The interior resembled a primate-themed rave. Banana peels, mango skins, and half-eaten sandwiches were strewn everywhere. The seats were ripped to shreds. The dashboard had been used as a launching pad for a free-for-all food fight. It was an absolute disaster. Those monkeys had ransacked my vehicle with the glee of a gang of pirates discovering a treasure chest brimming with loot. I was utterly flabbergasted and irate simultaneously. It took hours to clean up the mess, and the lingering scent of overripe fruit haunted my car for weeks. I learned a valuable lesson that day: never park under a flamboyant tree, especially if you value your automobile's pristine condition. The experience, though maddening, was so absurd that I couldn't help but chuckle about it afterward. I had to give them credit for their audacity; those little hooligans had style. On a different occasion, after a long flight back home from the States, I found a rather ominous note taped to my windshield. "We know where you live," it read, scrawled in what appeared to be dried blood. I nearly had a heart attack. Luckily, on closer inspection, the "blood" turned out to be ketchup, and the note itself was written by my perpetually mischievous younger brother. My family has always had a slightly warped sense of humor. I never know what to expect when returning home.

What screams "I'm pretending to be upper class"? I always get a chuckle when I hear someone with a pronounced working-class accent try to mimic the Queen's English. Like, I'm not saying that there's anything intrinsically wrong with having a working-class accent—it's just that the contrast between the carefully constructed, almost theatrical upper-class pronunciation and the natural, unvarnished tones of the street is often quite comical. Similarly, those who affect a certain level of sophistication, perhaps by dropping a few French phrases here and there, or name-dropping a few obscure European artists, yet are completely oblivious to the nuances of high society, give off the same air. Likewise, someone who suddenly begins using a plethora of obscure, archaic words in their everyday speech is instantly sussed.

What movies can you watch all the time and never get tired of watching? This is a tough one. I could probably watch *Pulp Fiction* and *So I Married an Axe Murderer* every single day and never get tired of them. *Pulp Fiction*, with its non-linear storytelling, quotable dialogue, and unforgettable characters, is a cinematic masterpiece that never fails to entertain. No matter how many times I see it, I always discover something new, a subtle nuance or a hidden joke that I missed before. The film's clever writing, expertly crafted by Quentin Tarantino, is a major reason for this. He blends violence, humor, and pop culture references into something truly unique, a symphony of cinematic delight. And then there is *So I Married an Axe Murderer*; a movie overflowing with quirky characters, slapstick comedy and subtle details of cultural "niche" humor. Its quick wit and self-aware absurdity are perfect for any occasion. I love how the movie understands the ridiculous nature of everyday life. It's the type of film that you can put on when you're feeling down and it will instantly lift your spirits.  However, that's just two movies. While the film list gets longer, it is nowhere near infinite. I find myself being able to watch most films over and over, but there are diminishing returns. At some point, the magic starts to wear off. The plot, pacing, and even the jokes lose their power. It’s like your favorite song, you might love it, but even the coolest track can be overplayed after a while. It’s a reminder that nothing lasts forever, even the best movies. So, while I have my go-to favorites, I’m always on the lookout for new films to add to the list and maybe even replace some of the old ones. Every year, there are new movies or even old movies which I've never heard of before that capture my attention. And who knows, maybe one day, I will find the perfect movie, the film that I can watch every single day and never get tired of. That's the dream, anyway.

I got an invitation to a high school reunion where I was bullied. I am successful in my career. I want the satisfaction that I’m doing better than my bullies, but I don’t want to demean myself on that level. Should I go? The quandary you've presented resonates with a discomforting familiarity, a societal pressure cookered into a question of validation. I've pondered this, the allure of the reunion, the yearning for that vindicating glance, the silent acknowledgment of ‘look at me now’. On one hand, the desire to flaunt one's triumph over one's past oppressors is a powerful motivator. It’s the raw, almost primal urge to show the naysayers, the tormentors, the ones who underestimated you, that their actions, their words, their very existence in your life, did not define or diminish you. You are now a testament to resilience. A shining beacon of "I told you so" without uttering a single word. Then there's the other side. The risk of debasement. The fear of becoming what you so vehemently despise. The reunion is a cage. It’s a performance. And do you really want to dedicate an evening to re-entering that cage, reliving the painful chapters of your life simply to receive fleeting gratification? You've already won. You've achieved success on your own terms. To attend such an event is a capitulation; a tacit admission that their approval is vital, that their past holds power over your present. That is a waste of time, and energy. If what it is you desire is gratification over the bullies, then it’s better to be the master of your own destiny by avoiding such a spectacle.

Why would homeless people rather beg on the street than get a job at McDonald’s? A question I frequently ponder, as one who's lived in a country teeming with both the visibly destitute and the readily available opportunities. The simplistic, often dehumanizing take is that the homeless are inherently lazy, preferring the perceived ease of panhandling to the discipline of regular employment. However, the situation is far more nuanced, a complex tapestry woven with threads of societal neglect, mental health issues, addiction, and the sheer, soul-crushing weight of systemic barriers. The notion that a minimum-wage job at a fast-food chain like McDonald’s represents a viable escape route for everyone is a fallacy; it's a misinformed perspective. For starters, securing such employment requires certain prerequisites that many homeless individuals lack — stable housing, an address, reliable transportation, and the ability to adhere to a rigid work schedule. Without any support, all of those things are impossible to get. Furthermore, the nature of homelessness itself can act as a significant impediment. Chronic sleep deprivation, the constant struggle for basic survival, and the psychological toll of living on the streets can make it difficult to maintain the focus and energy needed for sustained employment. Many also grapple with mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Their symptoms can sabotage any attempt to integrate into a structured work environment and these things may require medication that is often unavailable. The cycle of homelessness, mental illness, and unemployment can become vicious, making it increasingly difficult for individuals to break free. There may simply be no choice in matters as they see it.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? My late grandmother’s best friend, Lucille, was the undisputed master of the subtle culinary comeuppance. Lucille had a penchant for baking, and her coconut-based sweet bread was a staple at every family gathering. But, alas, her generosity was often exploited by a certain cousin. This cousin, let's call him "Reginald," was a charming rogue with a sweet tooth that could melt steel. Reginald, regardless of the occasion, would invariably sneak into the kitchen, swipe a generous slice (or two, or three) of Lucille’s prized sweet bread from under his very nose and make off with it. He would then feign innocence, declaring that he hadn’t touched a thing. Lucille, a woman of unwavering patience, tolerated this for years, her only concession being a slightly strained smile and a knowing glance toward her grandson. One day, however, the bread was a bit saltier than usual. The following week, it had an unexpected, but not necessarily unpleasant, addition of cayenne pepper. Eventually, Reginald had a nasty bout of diarrhea. He was at once mortified and suspicious. The following event at Lucille’s house, nobody touched the sweet bread. It tasted as good as ever. Lucille just simply gave one of her rare, but always knowing smiles. Reginald kept a safe distance.

Who is an actor who you think looks better older than they did when they were younger? Harrison Ford. There. I said it. I am old enough to be a child of the 70s when Harrison Ford was at his dashingly handsome peak. Han Solo. Indiana Jones. Rick Deckard. All iconic roles. Now, I'm not saying he wasn't good-looking back then, but there was a certain blandness to him, a kind of Hollywood studio-manufactured handsomeness that, whilst undeniably pleasing to the eye, didn't quite set the world ablaze. Then came age, and with it, the weathering of time, the crinkling of the skin, the silvering of the hair, the deepening of the lines etched into his face from a life well-lived. He now exudes a ruggedness, a gravitas, a world-weariness that only comes with the passage of years. He's become a proper leading man. He's less a pretty face and more a presence. And that presence is captivating. It's as if he's earned his attractiveness, paid his dues. I've always believed there is inherent glamour when it comes to senior citizens. Maybe it is because there is a lack of time, the knowledge that whatever happens, happens soon. Or maybe you are staring at someone who has been through hell and back and still has the conviction and will to push through whatever happens. Either or, I believe Harrison Ford is a testament to the fact that some things, indeed, do get better with age. He is like a perfectly aged whiskey, whose character becomes richer, bolder, more complex with each passing year.

My girlfriend is mad at me for "not standing up for her.” She accidentally spilled her drink on a girl in the club. The other girl threw her drink on my girlfriend and her boyfriend shoved me. I grabbed my girlfriend and we left. What should I do? This situation is a bit of a pickle, isn’t it? First off, before you go any further with anything or start taking sides, you need to understand her perspective completely. Ask her what she wanted you to do, and more importantly, why? Was it the initial spill, the reciprocation, or the physical shove that got her riled up? Try to get to the root of the problem. Sometimes it’s less about the incident itself and more about the underlying feelings of vulnerability or needing someone to have your back.  Now, let’s break it down. Realistically, violence is not the answer. If you started swinging, you’d likely escalate the situation and involve the police. The best thing you did was to remove yourselves from the situation. But maybe, standing up for her meant more than just physical confrontation. Maybe she wanted you to verbally defend her, back her up, even if it meant arguing with the other couple. Perhaps she expected you to act as a buffer, de-escalate the tension before it got physical. Maybe she just wanted you to have her back morally. These are all things you need figure out.

What advice changed your life financially? I don't recall any particular moment, conversation, or well-placed tip that revolutionized my financial life. However, I stumbled upon a sort of philosophy, or rather, a set of principles, that drastically altered my financial trajectory. It wasn't about specific stocks, real estate, or crypto, but about a fundamental reshaping of my mindset. The advice wasn't spoken, but rather absorbed through observation and, in some respects, sheer necessity. It was born out of being raised in a household where money was a perennially tight, a constant source of tension and anxiety. From a very young age, I realized that financial insecurity wasn't just something that affected adults; it permeated every aspect of life from what we ate to how we dressed.

What has an employee said that immediately caused you to fire them? I've never been in a position to fire anyone, thankfully. However, I have witnessed what would be considered automatic termination offenses. I worked in an environment for many years where one slight misstep was enough to render a person jobless. The type of workplace where, if there was one tiny incident, the owners took the "better safe than sorry" approach and simply got rid of you. This wasn't the case for all employees. There was an unspoken, unwritten rule that certain individuals had a far longer leash than others. Management’s friends and family were untouchable, of course. Some people, though, just by virtue of the temperament and perceived value, were allowed to get away with practically anything. The rest of us had to be on our toes, all the time. In this culture, the simplest mistake could be a career-ender. I was a junior staffer in an IT firm.

What movies do you like but everybody hates, and why? In the cinematic realm, there exists a peculiar cadre: films that, for whatever unfathomable reason, are universally reviled yet hold a special, almost guilty, pleasure for a select few. One such film for me is *Showgirls* (1995). Yes, *Showgirls*! I already know I'm inviting scorn by even mentioning this notorious NC-17 debacle. It is critically panned. A box office bomb. Accused of everything from atrocious acting, clunky dialogue, and a ludicrous plot to gratuitous nudity and exploitation of its female leads. Yet, I unabashedly love this movie. It's not a "so bad, it's good" kind of admiration. Granted, the acting is hammy, the dialogue is cringe-worthy, and the plot is as thin as a runway model. But there's something undeniably captivating about it. The film, a hyper-stylized, ultra-violent satire of a woman's relentless pursuit of stardom in the Las Vegas strip club scene. It could be the over-the-top performances, the campy aesthetic, Elizabeth Berkley's fierce commitment to her role as Nomi Malone, the audacity of Paul Verhoeven's direction, or the sheer, unfiltered excess of it all. It’s a guilty pleasure, a cinematic train wreck that I can't help but watch with a perverse grin. Or perhaps it's because the film is so utterly *unapologetic*. It doesn't feign subtlety or sophistication. It embraces its trashiness with a level of bravado that's almost admirable. It's a cinematic middle finger to the very notion of good taste. It is a film that one could interpret as a sharp indictment of the entertainment industry's superficiality and exploitation. And the film offers a fascinating, albeit exaggerated, peek behind the curtains of a specific subculture. Yes, I understand why most people loathe *Showgirls*. But I, for one, stand defiantly on the side of the guilty.

What disturbing rumor turned out to be true at your school? The one everyone spoke about in hushed tones was the existence of a secret gambling ring operating within the school. At first it was dismissed as mere adolescent fantasy, the fever dreams of students bored with quadratic equations and mandatory sports. The tales of high-stakes poker games held in the darkened confines of the library, whispered among the lockers, seemed too outlandish, too cinematic. The rumors gained traction over time, fueled by the sudden influx of expensive sneakers and electronic gadgets sported by a select group of students who had previously known only the thrift store. The ringleader was rumored to be the son of a wealthy landowner, a charismatic and notoriously cynical student with an eye for business, who seemed to glide through the halls, a smirk perpetually playing on his lips. He was the one who knew the right people to tap into the school's nascent underground economy. The rumors finally came to fruition when the principal, a stout, humorless woman with a penchant for draconian discipline, announced an investigation. Lockers were searched, and the school became a hive of suspicion and whispers. The news came out in drips and drabs: a few students were suspended, some were expelled, and the ringleader, in dramatic fashion, simply vanished, never to be seen or heard from within the school again. His absence caused a ripple effect. The school went through a period of paranoia, with a distinct chill in the air. Parents were suddenly monitoring their children's spending habits with hawk-like intensity, and teachers became more rigid in their rules and standards. In light of this I found that this was one of the many reasons why I never took school seriously. It was a constant reminder that the world beyond the classroom walls was far more complex and, frankly, far more interesting.

Which TV shows were popular when you were younger that would flop today? Why? As a child of the 80s and 90s, television was a foundational element in the construction of my personality, and the shows of my youth provided a constant, comforting backdrop to my existence. Looking back, some shows that were immensely popular then, I believe, would struggle mightily to gain traction today. Consider, for instance, the syndicated action-adventure series *Airwolf*. The premise -- a high-tech helicopter used for covert operations -- was undeniably cool, and the aerial stunts were impressive for their time. But the plots were often formulaic, the acting was wooden, and the visual effects, while groundbreaking then, now look laughably dated. Audiences, particularly younger ones, are far more sophisticated today. Shows like *Airwolf* would be seen as campy and slow-paced, lacking the narrative complexity and visual dynamism that viewers now expect. Furthermore, there's the issue of accessibility.  In an era of streaming services and on-demand content, the episodic structure of shows like *Airwolf* feels archaic. Modern viewers have little patience for episodes that don't advance a larger narrative or offer immediate gratification. The shows I grew up with, such as *Knight Rider* and *The A-Team*, thrived on formulaic plots, their appeal stemming from their comforting predictability. The plots were simple, the action was over the top (if you could call it that), and there was a reassuring sense that everything would be resolved within a sixty minute time slot. Today’s audiences, bombarded with a constant stream of new content, have evolved beyond this. They demand shows that challenge them, that offer intricate storylines, complex characters, and visually arresting presentations. The reliance on practical effects in those old series wouldn't cut it anymore. Contemporary audiences have become accustomed to the seamless integration of CGI and sophisticated visual storytelling, which would render these shows of yore almost unwatchable. Nostalgia, of course, would provide a certain allure, but realistically, these shows would struggle mightily to captivate a new generation of viewers.

The Good, the Bad & the Ugly is an amazing movie but I never understood the scene involving Tuco and his monk brother. As much as it was an emotional scene, it did not advance the movie plot at all. Did Leone ever explain why he added the scene? I've always found the scene somewhat jarring, a bit off-kilter amidst all the grit and gunfire. It’s like a sudden, unexpected dip into a different kind of story, a quieter, more introspective space that doesn't quite mesh with the rest of the film's bombastic energy. It's a moment of genuine vulnerability amidst all the bravado, and, perhaps, that's the point. It offers a glimpse into Tuco's humanity, his desperate need for connection, his longing for redemption. That scene wasn't there for plot advancement. I suspect Leone understood that films are not just about the plot. He understood there is a human aspect that is vital to the complete story. The scene is simply there to show us sides of the characters that we will never see in other scenes: To see Tuco not as a scheming, violent bandit, but as a son and a brother is vital to the complexity of the movie. It’s almost as if Leone believed that these moments, however brief, were necessary to fully understand the characters, to see them not just as archetypes, but as fleshed-out, complicated individuals. I think that the scene serves as a poignant counterpoint to the film’s overall cynicism. The film, after all, is one that is filled with violence and greed, and this scene is a reminder that, even in such a brutal world, there is room for love, brotherhood and, at least for a fleeting moment, grace. Maybe its purpose was simply to make us pause, offering a brief respite from the brutal world of the American West.

What should I absolutely not do when visiting your country? Do not, under any circumstances, arrive in Trinidad and Tobago radiating pretension or an air of haughty superiority. We are a proud, albeit sometimes chaotic, people, and we have a keen sense for those who look down upon us, subtly or otherwise. Leave your presumptions at the airport; this is not a place to trot out your preconceived notions of efficiency, order, or proper decorum. We operate on island time, and we're not particularly keen on adhering to the strictures of punctuality or the diktats of rigid schedules. Don’t assume your experience will mirror what you've read in some glossy travel brochure. We are a complex blend of cultures, a melting pot of the Caribbean, and the experiences are as diverse as the people. Avoid the temptation to treat us as exhibits in some exotic museum or lab rats in a social experiment. Be open to the unpredictability, embrace the spontaneity, and, above all, be respectful of our customs. Don’t try to impose your standards on ours: this will land you in trouble. Resist the urge to lecture us on anything. We have a strong history of fiercely resisting outside interference. Don’t be a know-it-all foreigner. Especially, don't try to tell us what constitutes ‘Trini’ or ‘Tobagonian’ life. We know our own lives and culture way more than you ever will after a week or a month. It’s a surefire way to make a less-than-stellar first impression. Don’t assume that because we speak English that we will immediately comprehend or defer to you. Our English is peppered with a vernacular that can be difficult for the uninitiated to decode, and we are hardly obligated to kowtow to anyone. Be prepared to adjust, listen carefully, and, most importantly, be patient. Remember, a little humility goes a long way.
